docs.title: Home
docs.text:
import disp_xr as dxr

ds = dxr.open_disp("F11116/")                      # lazy (time, y, x), CRS attached
ds = dxr.chain(dxr.mask(ds, "recommended"))   # displacement from the first date
ds = dxr.rereference(ds, "median")
velocity = dxr.fit_velocity(ds, method="midas")    # robust, with a sigma per pixel

docs.title: disp-xr
docs.text:
Xarray tools for OPERA surface displacement. Open a frame of DISP-S1 or DISP-NISAR granules as one lazy dataset, chain the ministacks, check quality, estimate velocities with honest uncertainties, compare with GNSS, downsample and export, from a laptop to an AWS Batch cluster.

Get started Tutorials API reference

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Open and chain frames

    Local folders, S3 or HTTPS; ministacks chained across reference dates and across product changes; virtual frames that open in seconds.

    Getting started

  • Quality and references

    Product masks, quality weights from similarity, coherence and inversion residuals, six reference methods, ionosphere and plate-motion corrections.

    Quality tutorials

  • Velocities and time series

    Trajectory fits, OLS, Whittle, MIDAS and GLS velocities with colored-noise sigmas, model diagnostics, Kalman and LOWESS denoising.

    Choosing a velocity method

  • GNSS validation

    Stations next to DISP through geepers, residuals against OPERA requirements, a GNSS tie that removes long-wavelength error.

    Comparing with GNSS

  • Downsample

    Quality-weighted grids, hexagons (planar and H3) and quadtrees, with cell uncertainties that account for spatial correlation.

    Downsampling

  • Export and serve

    Zarr v3, NetCDF, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, MintPy, Icechunk, GeoZarr for bowser, web map tiles, and region jobs for AWS Batch.

    Large frames and batch jobs

docs.title: API policy
docs.text: What disp-xr promises about its interface, its outputs and the products it reads, and how changes are made. The core API is frozen from 0.4.0, after the API review of 2026-10-11 (plan task T18): see "Frozen names" at the end. The freeze was planned for v0.2; no v0.2.0 was tagged, and v0.3.0 shipped before the review.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
disp-xr follows Semantic Versioning:

Release May contain Patch (1.2.3 → 1.2.4) Bug fixes and documentation only. Results change only where they were wrong. Minor (1.2 → 1.3) New features, new optional parameters, deprecations. Existing code keeps working, with warnings for deprecated names. Major (1 → 2) Removals of deprecated names and other breaking changes.

Before 1.0, a minor release (0.2 → 0.3) may also break the API, but only through the deprecation process below. Defaults chosen by trade studies (for example the quadtree split metric and quality-weight parameters of plan task T29) may still change before 1.0; each change is listed in the changelog with the study that motivated it.

docs.title: What is public
docs.text:
These are public, and covered by this policy:

  • the names in disp_xr.__all__, including the submodules it lists (disp_xr.gnss, disp_xr.models, disp_xr.diagnostics);
  • the public names of disp_xr.residuals, disp_xr.timeseries, disp_xr.batch, disp_xr.plot, disp_xr.search, disp_xr.weights, disp_xr.geometry and disp_xr.tutorial (those without a leading underscore, listed in each module's __all__);
  • the .disp accessor methods;
  • the disp_xr command, its subcommands and options;
  • the keys of disp_xr.config and their DISP_XR_* environment variables;
  • the layout of the stores disp-xr writes: variable names, dimension names, units, and the provenance attributes (history, input_granules, reference, product, frame_id).

Modules and names starting with an underscore are private and may change in any release. So are the deprecated module aliases (disp_xr.io, disp_xr.download, disp_xr.quality_metrics, disp_xr.static_layers, disp_xr.mintpy, disp_xr.utils), which are removed at 1.0.

docs.title: Stability levels
docs.text: Level Meaning Currently Stable Covered by everything above. Everything public not listed below Provisional May change in a minor release, with a changelog entry but without a deprecation cycle. DISP-NISAR support (product spec not yet validated, plan task T35); disp_xr.batch (region jobs); the REST service (disp_xr.serve, disp_xr serve; plan task T40)

docs.title: Deprecation
docs.text:
A renamed or removed public name:

  1. keeps working for at least one minor release (before 1.0) or until the next major release (after 1.0), emitting a DeprecationWarning that names its replacement;
  2. is listed under "Deprecated" in the changelog of the release that deprecates it, and under "Removed" in the release that removes it;
  3. is covered by a test that checks the warning and the forwarded result.

A change to a default value follows the same process when it changes results, except that defaults set by a documented trade study may change before 1.0 with a changelog entry (see "Versions").

docs.title: Supported products
docs.text:
Product Versions read Status DISP-S1 0.10 to below 2 Validated against production granules. Frames that span the November 2025 production change (float64 displacement, time stored as seconds since 2010) are read together, with a MixedPrecisionWarning; see Product notes. Version 0.10 (pre-release stakeholder runs) is read but not validated. DISP-NISAR 0.4 to below 2 Provisional: the spec follows SAS test output and is validated when real products are available (plan task T35).

Granules outside these ranges are refused with UnsupportedProductVersionError; open_disp(min_version=...) narrows the range further. A new product version is supported in a minor release, after its granules pass the test suite; the product notes record what changed.

docs.title: Supported Python and dependencies
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 and newer; the test matrix covers 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14.
  • Core dependencies follow the SPEC 0 schedule of the scientific Python ecosystem: a dependency version is supported for at least two years after its release.
  • Optional features live in extras (aws, cloud, gnss, plot, interactive, hex, eof, mintpy, jax, serve); a missing extra raises an ImportError that names it.

docs.title: Frozen names
docs.text:
Frozen from 0.4.0. Renaming or removing any of these, or changing a default that changes results, follows the deprecation process above.

Functions and classes (disp_xr.__all__):

  • Find and open: find_products, open_disp, open_disp_tree, open_static, open_icechunk, open_virtual, open_pyramid, build_virtual_frame, validate_virtual, and search_granules (resolved on first use; needs the aws extra).
  • Prepare: correct, remove_plate_motion, mask, valid_mask, quality_summary, quality_weights, chain, NaNPolicy, rereference, rechunk, to_units, validate_disp, enu_to_los.
  • Analyse: fit_velocity, fit_trajectory, predict_trajectory, Trajectory, fit_noise, NoiseResult, denoise, downsample, downsample_hex, quadtree, Quadtree, to_points, to_geodataframe, empirical_variogram, fit_variogram, VariogramModel, and the submodules gnss, models, diagnostics.
  • Write: to_zarr, to_netcdf, to_geotiff, to_mintpy, to_geozarr, to_pyramid, build_overviews, to_icechunk.
  • config, __version__.

Accessor (ds.disp): chain, correct, mask, remove_plate_motion, rereference, rechunk, denoise, deramp, quality_summary, to_units, plot_map, plot_point, validate, and the properties history and grid.

Command line: disp_xr info, stack, export, geometry, search, virtual and serve (provisional, with the REST service).

Conventions decided in the review:

Convention Rule Chaining chain / .disp.chain() Default corrections correct(ds) subtracts what the product has not applied (which="product") Existing outputs Every writer takes overwrite: bool = False and refuses an existing output unless it is set; to_icechunk keeps mode for appends NaN at a crossover nan_policy="omit" carries the offset accumulated before the gap Chunk layouts rechunk names its layout; there is no default Order of steps .disp.mask() and .disp.correct() refuse chained data

Deprecated, removed in 1.0: stack_disp and .disp.stack() (use chain); rechunk without a layout; mode= on to_zarr, to_geozarr and to_pyramid (use overwrite); combine_disp_product, rebase_disp, create_rebased_displacement, get_disp_info; the module aliases listed under "What is public".

docs.title: View in bowser
docs.text:
bowser is a web viewer for InSAR displacement stacks. to_geozarr writes a GeoZarr store that bowser opens directly, without its tifs-to-geozarr converter:

import disp_xr as dxr

ds = dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp("granules/")).disp.rereference("auto")
dxr.to_geozarr(ds, "frame.zarr", static=dxr.open_static(ds), factors=(33, 67))

or from the command line:

disp_xr export frame_stack.zarr --format geozarr --out frame.zarr --static-dir static/
bowser run --stack-file frame.zarr

docs.title: What the store holds
docs.text:
• A multiscale pyramid: level 0 at 30 m, display levels by factor 2 until the shorter side is under 256 cells (as bowser's own converter builds them), and any analysis levels given in factors, all quality-weighted means (downsample). bowser picks the level whose pixel matches the map tile, so a pyramid of only 33, 67 and 333 would make mid zooms read 30 m.
  • Every level is a complete dataset with the same variables (plus the cell statistics on coarse levels), its own CRS and transform.
  • Float32 data, chunks of one epoch by 256 x 256 pixels in shards of four epochs by 1,024 x 1,024 (bowser's tile-read layout).

docs.title: What bowser reads, and what disp-xr sets for it
docs.text: bowser reads disp-xr writes Root multiscales.layout[].asset, finest first The zarr-conventions multiscales v0.1 layout (also derived_from, transform, spatial:transform, spatial:shape) CRS from proj:code, then proj:wkt2, then spatial_ref.crs_wkt All three, on the root and on every level Geometry from pixel-center x/y (y descending) and GeoTransform Both, recomputed per level Whether to offer a moving reference point: bowser_uses_spatial_ref, else the units (meters, radians) bowser_uses_spatial_ref on every variable: true only for displacement and velocity. Without it, bowser would re-reference sigmas (meters) and inversion residuals (radians) Colorbar title from long_name, unit from units Both on every variable Reference marker from reference_lonlat The point chosen by rereference (none for a median or area reference) Line-of-sight panel from heading_angle_deg, incidence_angle_deg, los_enu_ground_to_satellite Near, center and far values from the static layers, when static is given; the heading assumes a right-looking radar unless look_side="left" Histogram panel from bowser_histogram (else it reads a full epoch per request) Per-epoch bins and percentiles on level 0, computed once at write time Masks from temporal_coherence, phase_similarity, recommended_mask, on the level being drawn Present on every level (masks by mode, quality layers by weighted mean)

docs.title: Best practices that do not affect bowser
docs.text:
These are checked against bowser ops (0a61c6a: zarr 3.1.1, xarray 2025.8, rioxarray 0.19) by tests/bowser_check.py, which runs bowser's own server on a store and requests the dataset list, tiles at every level with and without a mask, a point, a chart, the histogram and the range:

Practice bowser proj: and spatial: attributes on every level, not only level 0 Ignored; no effect Multiscales transform and derived_from Ignored; no effect Consolidated metadata at the root bowser opens with consolidated=False; no effect spatial_ref as a coordinate (bowser's converter writes a data variable) Found as before ("spatial_ref" in ds.variables) Integer masks with a _FillValue instead of float NaN xarray decodes the fill to NaN on read; masks and histograms behave as with floats Small levels stored as one chunk Read as usual Coarse levels with extra variables (sigma, n_eff, ...) Not listed (bowser lists level 0); harmless Dataset attributes as JSON objects (reference_lonlat, LOS) Required: as JSON strings, bowser fails to read the LOS attributes. disp-xr writes JSON objects to Zarr (NetCDF keeps strings)

Gaps in bowser found on the way, not fixed here: overview levels written by its converter have no proj:/spatial: attributes; it never reads spatial:*; it chooses the level by comparing the pixel size in native CRS units with Web Mercator meters, so a geographic-CRS store always gets the coarsest level; and it has no Zarr tests. disp-xr stores are UTM, so the level choice works.

docs.title: Testing against bowser
docs.text:
cd bowser && pixi install -e test --frozen
DISP_XR_BOWSER_PYTHON=$PWD/.pixi/envs/test/bin/python \
    pixi run -e test pytest tests/test_geozarr.py   # in disp-xr

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The disp_xr command wraps the library for batch runs; each subcommand calls the functions of the same name. disp_xr --debug <command> logs debug messages and shows tracebacks instead of one-line errors. Every command has --help.

disp_xr info PATHS...      [--frame-id F] [--min-version V] [--json] [--table granules.csv]
disp_xr stack PATHS... --out out.zarr|out.nc
    [--corrections product|none|ionospheric_delay,solid_earth_tide]
    [--mask recommended|strict|none]
    [--reference auto|point|median|border|high_coherence|none]
    [--row R --col C | --lon X --lat Y] [--start DATE --end DATE]
    [--preset timeseries|maps] [--overwrite]
disp_xr export PATHS... --format cog|geotiff|zarr|geozarr|netcdf|mintpy --out OUT
    [--layer displacement] [--epoch DATE | --per-epoch] [--static-dir DIR] [--overwrite]
disp_xr geometry PATHS... --out static.zarr [--static-dir DIR] [--no-download]
disp_xr search --frame-id F [--start DATE] [--end DATE] [--product DISP-S1|DISP-NISAR]
    [--version 1.0|any] [--url-type https|s3] [--out granules.csv]
disp_xr virtual PATHS... --repo DIR [--branch main] [--workers N] [--no-validate]
disp_xr serve STORES...    [--host 127.0.0.1] [--port 9000] [--no-tiles]

docs.title: A typical run
docs.text:
disp_xr info granules/                                  # what is there
disp_xr stack granules/ --out frame.zarr --mask strict  # correct, mask, chain, reference
disp_xr export frame.zarr --format cog --out last.tif   # Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
disp_xr export frame.zarr --format mintpy --out mintpy/
disp_xr export frame.zarr --format geozarr --out view.zarr  # bowser opens it
  • stack runs the steps in the fixed order: corrections and quality mask per granule, chaining, re-referencing. --corrections product (the default) subtracts the corrections the product has not applied already.
  • export takes a store written by stack, or granules, which it chains without corrections, masking or re-referencing.
  • An existing output is refused unless --overwrite is given.
  • geometry and search need the aws extra; virtual needs cloud; serve needs serve.
  • serve names each dataset after its store (frame.zarr is frame) and serves it read-only under /datasets/<name>/disp/: timeseries, velocity, cells, gnss and provenance. The API page is at /docs.

docs.title: Granules and frames
docs.text: A DISP granule is one NetCDF file holding the displacement between two dates, a reference date and a secondary date, on a fixed grid called a frame. A DISP-S1 frame is about 7,000 x 9,000 pixels at 30 m in a UTM zone. A frame's history is a few hundred granules.

docs.title: Ministacks and reference dates
docs.text:
The processor (dolphin) works on ministacks: blocks of about 15 acquisitions that share one reference date. Every granule in a ministack measures displacement from that ministack's reference date, so the raw series restarts at zero at each new ministack.

The next ministack's reference date is the last secondary date of the previous one. That shared epoch, the crossover, links them: chain adds to each ministack the displacement accumulated at its crossover, so the whole series becomes relative to the first reference date. A missing crossover granule breaks the chain, and chain raises MissingCrossoverError. A NaN at a crossover makes later epochs of that pixel NaN (nan_policy="propagate", the default).

open_disp returns the series as stored, relative to each ministack reference; reference_time says which one. chain returns it chained, with attrs["reference_date"] set and a zero epoch prepended at the first reference date.

docs.title: Spatial reference
docs.text: DISP displacement is relative to a reference point chosen by the processor. rereference subtracts, at every epoch, the value of a pixel you choose or the median of an area, so the series is relative to ground you trust.

docs.title: Units and sign
docs.text: Products store meters, positive toward the satellite (uplift or motion along the look direction toward it). to_units converts length layers to cm or mm; plots use mm by default.

docs.title: Quality layers
docs.text:
Each granule carries quality layers alongside displacement:

Layer Meaning recommended_mask 1 where the processor recommends the pixel temporal_coherence, phase_similarity 0 to 1; higher is better connected_component_labels unwrapping regions; 0 is unreliable water_mask 0 over water persistent_scatterer_mask 1 for persistent scatterers shp_counts, estimated_phase_quality, timeseries_inversion_residuals diagnostics

mask sets displacement to NaN where pixels fail: the "recommended" preset uses recommended_mask, "strict" adds connected components, water and a temporal-coherence threshold. quality_summary maps how often each pixel passes.

docs.title: Corrections
docs.text: The /corrections group holds the ionospheric delay and solid-earth tide that the processor estimated but did not subtract. correct subtracts them once, before chaining, and records what it applied; it refuses a correction the product already applied (DISP-NISAR ionosphere).

docs.title: Chunks
docs.text:
Data is opened lazily in the layout of the files: one epoch and one block per dask chunk (chunks="native"). Each operation then reads what it needs:

Question Reads a map of one epoch that epoch, plus one crossover epoch per earlier ministack a pixel's time series one block from every granule a per-pixel fit rechunks to whole time series itself

rechunk switches layouts when one kind of access repeats. Stores written with to_zarr choose their layout with preset=: "timeseries" for per-pixel work, "maps" for maps.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page goes from a folder of DISP granules to a referenced displacement time series, a map and an export. Every block runs as written: the first one writes a small synthetic frame with disp_xr.tutorial, so nothing needs downloading. Replace the path with your own granules.

docs.title: Make or find granules
docs.text:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import disp_xr as dxr
from disp_xr.tutorial import make_disp_stack

folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "granules"
make_disp_stack(folder, "three_ministacks", shape=(128, 128))

table = dxr.find_products(folder)  # one row per granule, sorted by date
print(table[["frame_id", "reference_time", "secondary_time", "version"]])

find_products parses OPERA file names (and the /identification group when the name is not standard), drops duplicate granules keeping the latest version and production, and refuses unsupported product versions. On your own data it also accepts a glob, a list of paths or an s3:// prefix.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
ds = dxr.open_disp(table, corrections=True)
ds

ds is lazy: dims (time, y, x), coordinates time (secondary date) and reference_time (the ministack reference date of each epoch), the CRS from spatial_ref, and one variable per product layer. Integer layers keep their dtype and their no-data value; float layers use NaN.

docs.title: Correct, mask and chain
docs.text:
The order is fixed: corrections and the quality mask are applied per granule, before the ministacks are chained.

ds = dxr.correct(ds)                  # ionosphere and solid-earth tide
ds = dxr.mask(ds, "recommended")      # NaN where recommended_mask is bad
ds = dxr.chain(ds)               # one series from the first date
ds.attrs["reference_date"]

The accessor gives the same operations as methods, so a chain reads in order: ds.disp.correct().disp.mask("recommended").disp.chain().

docs.title: Re-reference
docs.text:
Displacement in DISP is relative to the product's reference point. Pick your own: a stable pixel chosen automatically, a point, the scene median, or an area.

ds = dxr.rereference(ds, "auto")          # deterministic stable pixel
# dxr.rereference(ds, "point", lon=-118.1, lat=34.2)
# dxr.rereference(ds, "area", bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax))

docs.title: Plot
docs.text:
ds.disp.plot_map()                     # last epoch, mm, symmetric scale
ds.disp.plot_point(row=64, col=64)     # series with reference changes marked

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
dxr.to_zarr(ds, folder.parent / "frame.zarr")          # Zarr v3, sharded
dxr.to_geotiff(ds.isel(time=-1), folder.parent / "last.tif", layer="displacement")  # COG

Every output records the disp-xr version, the input granules and the operations applied (ds.disp.history). The gallery shows each format, including MintPy.

docs.title: Large frames
docs.text: A full frame is about 7,000 x 9,000 pixels and a few hundred epochs. open_disp keeps the layout of the files, one epoch and one 1,024-pixel block per chunk, so a map or a point reads only what it needs. For repeated per-pixel work, rechunk once with ds.disp.rechunk("timeseries"), or write a Zarr copy with preset="timeseries". See Chunks for maps and time series.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: disp-xr needs Python 3.12 or newer.

docs.title: pip
docs.text: pip install "disp_xr @ git+https://github.com/mgovorcin/disp-xr"

docs.title: pixi (development)
docs.text:
pixi reads pyproject.toml and installs disp-xr in editable mode with pinned dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/mgovorcin/disp-xr.git
cd disp-xr
pixi install -e dev      # tests, linters and every extra
pixi run -e test test    # run the tests

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The core package opens, processes and exports local granules. Extras add the rest; install them with pip install "disp_xr[extra1,extra2]".

Extra Adds Needed for aws asf_search, s3fs, aiohttp, requests, shapely, dem_stitcher, tile_mate search, remote s3:// and https:// granules, static-layer and DEM downloads, polygon references plot matplotlib plot_map, plot_point mintpy mintpy reading the MintPy export with MintPy (writing it needs only h5py) cloud virtualizarr, icechunk, obstore to_icechunk, virtual stores jax jax jax_solve_linear_system gnss geepers GNSS series, LOS projection and DISP at stations (disp_xr.gnss) hex h3, geopandas H3 hexagons (downsample_hex(grid="h3")) and to_geodataframe eof xeofs EOF analysis (planned) interactive hvplot, datashader interactive full-frame browsing serve xpublish, xpublish-tiles, fastapi, uvicorn, pydantic the read-only REST service (disp_xr serve, disp_xr.serve) docs mkdocs and plugins building this site

Remote access needs Earthdata Login credentials in ~/.netrc (or the EARTHDATA_USERNAME and EARTHDATA_PASSWORD environment variables); S3 access inside AWS us-west-2 uses temporary ASF credentials fetched with them.

docs.title: Large frames and batch jobs
docs.text: A DISP-S1 frame is about 70 million pixels by hundreds of epochs, so how dask runs matters as much as the code. These settings come from running full frames on a 224-core, 1 TB node.

docs.title: Processes, not threads
docs.text:
Use a dask cluster of local processes for full frames:

from distributed import Client, LocalCluster

with LocalCluster(n_workers=24, threads_per_worker=1, memory_limit="8GB") as cluster, Client(cluster):
    ds = dxr.open_disp("F08882/")
    ...

Dask's default threaded scheduler runs at about one core on two common steps:

  • Reading granules. The HDF5 library holds a process-wide lock, so threads decompress NetCDF granules one at a time.
  • Reading Zarr. zarr decodes chunks in one thread per process.

On a full frame, rereference("auto") took half an hour on threads, because it reads every quality layer of every epoch.

docs.title: Memory and graph size
docs.text:
Measured on full DISP-S1 frames (2026-10-05):

  • Workers: 8 GB per worker was enough for every step of a full-frame study (open, chain, write, velocity, downsampling, quadtrees) with 16 to 24 workers; no worker paused, spilled or restarted.
  • Coordinator: the process that builds the graph and, with LocalCluster, runs the scheduler, holds the task graph. A frame prepared for writing is about 200,000 tasks and 35 MB pickled, and the process stays near 1 GB. (Before disp-xr 0.3 a frame-sized array of default weights was embedded in velocity graphs and pushed it to 80-100 GB.)
  • Opening: open_disp reads each granule's metadata, about 0.2 s per granule, so a 400-granule frame takes over a minute to open. Build a virtual frame once when you open the same frame repeatedly.
  • Task counts grow with epochs times spatial blocks times layers: one epoch per chunk by default, so downsampling a 389-epoch frame is about 2 million tasks, which the distributed scheduler handles.

Memory budget (decided 2026-10-06, plan task T37.1): 8 GB per worker and 4 GB for the coordinator. No worker of the full-frame T29 runs paused, spilled or restarted at 8 GB, and a frame prepared for writing peaks at about 1.2 GB on the coordinator.

docs.title: disp-xr settings
docs.text:
Each setting can be given in code (disp_xr.config.set({...})) or as an environment variable for batch jobs (DISP_XR_ plus the key in capitals, with __ for nested keys).

Setting Default What it does max_load_bytes 2 GB Largest array that export and plotting load into memory. Larger ones raise LoadTooLargeError, which names the size and what to do, before anything is read num_workers 32 Dask threads when disp-xr computes (plots, exports), unless dask's own num_workers is set. One per core (224) exhausted memory maps when reading a pixel series from hundreds of granules numba_threads 1 numba threads inside each dask task. numba starts one per core in every task, which crashed a 224-core node threads None BLAS threads inside each task for compiled kernels chunks.read_block 1024 Spatial block read from each granule chunks.target_mb 100 Target size of one dask chunk and Zarr shard

docs.title: Environment for batch jobs
docs.text:
These multiply with dask's own parallelism, so set them per job:

export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
export ZARR_ASYNC__CONCURRENCY=4      # zarr's default is 10 per thread
export DISP_XR_MAX_LOAD_BYTES=8000000000

ZARR_ASYNC__CONCURRENCY caps zarr's concurrent requests. Its default of 10 applies per dask thread, which floods object stores and local disks alike on large machines.

docs.title: Shared nodes: check memory first
docs.text:
On a busy shared node, fresh memory can stall in the kernel (transparent huge page compaction). Touching 2 GB then takes 40 s instead of half a second, and every step of a run slows by as much. Before timing anything, or when a run is unexpectedly slow, check:

python -c "import numpy as np, time; t = time.perf_counter(); np.ones(2**28); print(time.perf_counter() - t)"

A healthy node takes about 0.2 s. Ten times that means the run measures the node, not the code.

docs.title: Laziness
docs.text:
Building a result reads nothing. tests/test_lazy.py builds the core operations under a dask scheduler that refuses to compute. A few steps read small data on purpose:

  • open_disp reads reference_time;
  • to_points reads which cells hold data;
  • quadtree computes its split scores;
  • rereference(check_point=True) reads the reference pixel.

docs.title: Building a frame with region jobs
docs.text:
disp_xr.batch splits the build of a frame cube into independent jobs, one per region of whole shards, for AWS Batch array jobs or a pool of dask workers. The coordinator writes the store's metadata once and plans the jobs:

import json
import disp_xr as dxr
from disp_xr.batch import init_store, plan_jobs

granules = list(search_table["filename"])           # resolved once, here
template = dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp(granules))  # lazy: reads no pixel
shards = init_store(template, "s3://bucket/F11116.zarr")
jobs = plan_jobs(template, "s3://bucket/F11116.zarr", granules, shards)
with open("jobs.jsonl", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(job.to_json() + "\n" for job in jobs)

Each worker (AWS Batch array index i) runs one job and reports a result:

import os
from disp_xr.batch import RegionJob, run_region, write_manifest

line = open("jobs.jsonl").readlines()[int(os.environ["AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX"])]
job = RegionJob.from_json(line)
result = run_region(job, lambda ds, job: dxr.chain(dxr.mask(ds, "recommended")))
write_manifest([result], f"manifest-{job.job_id}.jsonl")

A job owns whole shards and overwrites them, so a retry is safe. Collect the manifests and resubmit what failed with failed_jobs(jobs, results).

Processing in a job must be local in space: masking, corrections, chaining and per-pixel fits work region by region. A spatial reference or a deramp needs the whole frame, so apply it afterwards on the assembled store, lazily:

cube = xr.open_zarr("s3://bucket/F11116.zarr").disp.rereference("median")
velocity = dxr.fit_velocity(cube, "midas")
cells = dxr.downsample(cube, factor=33)
report = dxr.residuals.compare(cells, dxr.gnss.load(cube), dxr.open_static(cube))

docs.title: Porting plan: opera_utils functions into disp-xr
docs.text:
disp-xr does not depend on opera_utils (PRD decision, Sep 30, 2026). The DISP product logic it needs is ported into disp-xr modules, with attribution, and disp-xr owns and tests it from then on.

  • Source: opera-utils commit 97f77d9 (upstream opera-adt/opera-utils main, 2026-06-04). The port was read from a checkout at a fork commit, dff4b45, that adds only NISAR download modules on top of 97f77d9; every ported file and test is identical in the two, so headers cite the public 97f77d9.
  • Status of this spec: written by two readers of the source. The independent verification pass did not run; spot checks of the license, the filename regex, the module locations and upstream bugs 1–3 passed. Confirm every line range when porting.
  • Tasks: each row names the task in todo.md that owns the port.

docs.title: License and attribution
docs.text:
opera_utils is dual-licensed, BSD-3-Clause or Apache-2.0, at the user's choice (Copyright (c) 2022 California Institute of Technology, U.S. Government sponsorship acknowledged). disp-xr is BSD-3-Clause, so the ports are taken under BSD-3-Clause.

  1. Ship the opera_utils BSD-3-Clause text as LICENSES/opera-utils-BSD-3-Clause.txt, and list it under license-files in pyproject.toml so it goes into the sdist, wheel and conda package.
  2. Give each ported module a header: Portions adapted from opera-utils (https://github.com/opera-adt/opera-utils, commit 97f77d9, <source path>), Copyright (c) 2022 California Institute of Technology, BSD-3-Clause; modified for disp-xr.
  3. Do not use the Caltech or JPL names to endorse disp-xr.
  4. Ported tests carry the same header.
  5. plate_motion.py follows MintPy code, and MintPy is GPL-3.0. Do not copy it. Reimplement plate motion from the published math (ITRF2014 plate motion model, Altamimi et al. 2017) and cite the paper.
  6. A CI rule forbids import opera_utils (ruff TID251 banned-api), so the dependency cannot come back.

docs.title: Upstream bugs to fix in the ports
docs.text:
Each gets a regression test in disp-xr.

  1. DispProductStack sorts versions as strings, so 1.10 ranks below 1.9.
  2. search() drops the frame filter when product_version=None.
  3. create_rebased_displacement(add_reference_time=True) labels the zero epoch with the first secondary time, giving a duplicate time coordinate.
  4. rebase_timeseries accumulates in float32 whatever the input dtype, and never checks that the crossover epoch exists.
  5. get_reference_values: the point method has no bounds check (negative indices wrap), the median ignores good_pixel_mask, and high_coherence with no mask silently uses every pixel.
  6. mintpy._write_hdf5 leaves compression off for every dataset after the first; the metadata hard-codes Sentinel-1 platform, wavelength and height, and the velocity step loads the full cube.
  7. plate_motion.geodetic_to_ecef passes radians to a transformer that expects degrees.
  8. plate_motion.run swaps latitude and longitude when unpacking the mesh grid.

docs.title: Practices kept from opera_utils
docs.text:
• Processing order: corrections, then quality mask (both per product, before chaining), then chain, then spatial reference. Masked NaNs then propagate through the chain.
  • NaNPolicy.propagate is the default.
  • Chain with the whole time axis in one chunk and spatial chunks clamped to the array shape.
  • Use ds.rio.transform(), not the GeoTransform attribute, after subsetting.
  • Read /identification and /metadata with h5py; xarray cannot decode their byte strings.
  • Zarr v3 output with inner chunks plus shards, dask rechunked to the shard shape before writing, and uncompressed coordinates.

docs.title: Tests to port
docs.text:
All are synthetic and need no network: test_disp_rebase.py, test_disp_reference.py, the combine_quality_masks and encoding parts of test_disp_reformat.py, test_disp_utils.py (mantissa rounding, chunk clamping, NetCDF encoding), the filename and dedupe parts of test_disp_product.py, test_disp_search.py (mocked requests), test_disp_remote.py and test_credentials.py (monkeypatched).

mintpy.py, plate_motion.py, create_incidence_range.py and stitch_geometry_layers have no upstream tests; the ports need new ones.

docs.title: Product notes
docs.text: Differences between DISP productions that affect reading a frame, found while using real frames. Each note says what changed, how it was found and what disp-xr does about it.

docs.title: DISP-S1 displacement precision: float32 before November 2025, float64 after
docs.text:
What changed. DISP-S1 granules produced in November 2025 and later store the displacement layer as float64. Earlier productions store it as float32. No other layer changes: the corrections, short_wavelength_displacement, the quality layers and the masks have the same dtype, chunks and compression in every production.

Not a reprocessing. The later granules continue the time series rather than replace it. In frame F11116 (central California), the April 2025 production ends at 2024-10-03. The first November 2025 granule is a ministack referenced on that date (20241003T140837Z_20241015T140837Z). A time series that runs past October 2024 therefore needs both productions.

How it was found. The split-metric study (T29, 2026-10-04) downloaded all 389 F11116 granules from CMR. open_disp refused them with MixedProductionError:

Production Granules displacement Secondary dates April 2025 314 float32 2016-07-05 to 2024-10-03 November 2025 45 float64 from 2024-10-15 August 2026 30 float64 to 2026-04-26

Every 2D layer of one granule from each production was compared with h5py:

displacement  float32  float64  float64
same: connected_component_labels, corrections/ionospheric_delay,
      corrections/perpendicular_baseline, corrections/solid_earth_tide,
      estimated_phase_quality, persistent_scatterer_mask, phase_similarity,
      recommended_mask, short_wavelength_displacement, shp_counts,
      temporal_coherence, timeseries_inversion_residuals, water_mask

What disp-xr does. open_disp reads granules that differ only in the precision of a float layer:

  • it raises a MixedPrecisionWarning that lists each production;
  • it casts the layer to float32 (float32 resolves about 10 nm on a 10 cm displacement);
  • it records the layer in attrs["mixed_precision"].

Any other difference (an integer layer becoming float, a new fill value, other compression or chunks) still raises MixedProductionError. So does build_virtual_frame, because a virtual store references the stored chunks and needs one dtype per array.

import warnings
import disp_xr as dxr
from disp_xr.product import MixedPrecisionWarning

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", MixedPrecisionWarning)  # once you know
    ds = dxr.open_disp("F11116/")
ds.attrs["mixed_precision"]  # ['displacement']

docs.title: DISP-S1 time encoding changed in November 2025
docs.text:
What changed. The same productions also encode time and reference_time differently. The earlier granules store 0 seconds since the acquisition time itself (seconds since 2024-10-03 14:08:37.435763), which decodes exactly. The later granules store float seconds since 2010 (seconds since 2010-01-01 00:00:00.000000), which decodes a few nanoseconds off: 2024-10-03 14:08:37.435763008.

Why it matters. Ministacks are chained through exact dates: each ministack's reference date must be an epoch of the previous one. In F11116 the November 2025 ministack references 2024-10-03, but that date read from the April 2025 granule differs by 8 ns, so chain raised MissingCrossoverError.

What disp-xr does. open_disp reads time and reference_time to the whole second (floored), as granule names give them (20241003T140837Z). Epochs of one frame are days apart, so nothing below a second is used.

docs.title: Open questions for OPERA
docs.text:
• Is the float64 displacement intended? Its granules are larger, and float32 already holds more precision than the measurement has.
  • Could the time encoding stay one style across productions?

docs.title: References and practices
docs.text:
Practices disp-xr follows, where each one comes from, and which task implements it. The PRD (specs.md) states the rules; this file holds the evidence and the detail.

How the list was built: one reader per repository read the source, docs and examples, and a second reader re-opened every cited file and tried to refute each claim. Only confirmed or corrected practices are listed. Where the reference code has a bug or a gap, it is listed under "Do not copy".

Adoption levels: core = disp-xr does this by default; opt-in = behind the cloud extra or a keyword; example = shown in the docs gallery only.

The conventions are still at pilot maturity (section 2), so the writer must be easy to migrate Core topozarr test_specs.py T27.7 Small levels (a frame at 1 km is about 250 x 300 pixels) use one spatial chunk over all of time Core icechunk-multiscales-demo T27.7 Keep the 30 m level virtual and materialize only the overviews Opt-in topozarr build_demo_data.py T27.7, T6.5b

Downsampling rules that came out of this reading:

  • Odd integer factors (33, 67, 333) keep cell centers on 30 m pixel centers. The demos use factor 2 only.
  • A weighted median is not composable; compute each level from 30 m. A mean is composable only with stored sum(w), and with NaNs a mean of block means is not the mean of the pixels.
  • Mask and label layers need mode or "any", not a mean.
  • Build overviews after chaining and re-referencing.

docs.text:

Practice Level Source Task Load time, reference_time, x, y and spatial_ref; keep only the data layers virtual Opt-in VirtualiZarr usage.md; icechunk-nasa write_virtual.ipynb T6.5b Concatenate with data_vars="all", coords="minimal", compat="override", join="exact". The DISP layers have no time dimension in the file, so data_vars="minimal" would keep only the first granule. Never forward the open_virtual_mfdataset defaults Core VirtualiZarr xarray.py; granule check T6.1, T6.5b Check dtype, chunk shape and codecs per layer before combining, and split a frame by production version Core icechunk-nasa design notes; VirtualiZarr writers/icechunk.py T5.8 Drop the /identification and /metadata string datasets; their lengths differ per file Core Granule check (dolphin_workflow_config is S64571 in one production and S78086 in another) T6.5b Open /corrections as a separate node; drop_variables is not forwarded into subgroups Opt-in VirtualiZarr hdf.py T6.5b The HDF parser holds the HDF5 lock, so use processes or batch jobs, not threads Opt-in VirtualiZarr scaling.md T6.5b Register a virtual chunk container for the source bucket; credentials for it are passed at open and are not saved with the repo Opt-in icechunk virtual.md; VirtualiZarr examples T6.5b Validate after every build: random pixel series and one full epoch against h5py reads Core icechunk-nasa design notes T6.5b Treat the virtual store as an ingest and index layer; write a native timeseries store for per-pixel work Core icechunk-nasa; VirtualiZarr caveats T6.5b, T14.2 Replace a reprocessed granule with a region write, not an append Opt-in VirtualiZarr accessor.py T6.5b

Facts about DISP-S1 granules found during this reading (to confirm in T2.2):

  • Data layers are chunked 256 x 256 with gzip level 4 and shuffle, which the HDF parser supports.
  • One frame has about 1,000 to 1,150 chunks per layer and 14 2D layers, so about 15,000 references per granule and a few million per frame.
  • time units were per-file in the 2025 production and fixed (seconds since 2010-01-01) in the 2026 production.
  • Displacement was float32 in a 2025 production granule and float64 in a 2026 one.

docs.title: 1.8 Do not copy
docs.text:
Bugs and gaps found in the reference code:

  • bowser (ops, 0a61c6a) writes proj:/spatial: attributes only on level 0 and the root, never reads spatial:*, derived_from or transform, chooses the level by comparing the pixel size in native CRS units with Web Mercator meters (so a geographic CRS always gets the coarsest level), keeps spatial_ref as a data variable, and has no Zarr tests. disp-xr writes every level self-contained, so its stores are readable by bowser and by strict GeoZarr readers. Verified on bowser's own server: none of disp-xr's extra metadata changes what bowser reads or shows, but dataset attributes must be JSON objects, not strings (see docs/bowser.md).
  • icechunk-multiscales-demo sets overview coordinates to the first pixel of each block while its transform implies block centers, and its array shapes (ceil) disagree with its coarsening (floor) when a size is not divisible.
  • topozarr coarsens by 2 only, with unweighted reductions and boundary="trim".
  • serverless-datacube-demo commits whatever sessions came back, even after failed jobs, and uses the pre-1.0 Icechunk distributed API.
  • cloud-tensor-storage-benchmarks times Icechunk writes without the commit, leaves one backend uncompressed while others use zstd, and never checks the data it reads.
  • workshop-cng-2025-zarr and icechunk-nasa pin pre-1.0 Icechunk and VirtualiZarr 1.x APIs; one workshop cell appends the wrong variable.

docs.title: 2. Zarr best practices
docs.text:
Source: zarr.dev and the documents it links: the zarr-python user guide, the Zarr v3 specification, the ZEPs and the zarr-conventions repositories. Read on Oct 1, 2026 by one reader; these rows were not independently re-checked.

Practice Source Task A chunk is the unit of reading and should be at least 1 MB uncompressed. Keep the dimension you read along whole and split the others. Float32 sizes: (300, 64, 64) is 4.9 MB, (300, 128, 128) is 19.7 MB, (1, 1024, 1024) is 4 MB performance guide T14.2 A shard is the unit of writing and must be written whole. Use sharding when small chunks would create too many objects. A 30 m frame layer at 300 epochs is about 84 GB, so shards of a few hundred MB keep the object count in the hundreds performance guide, sharding codec T14.2 Make one dask chunk equal one shard. The worker memory budget must hold one uncompressed shard plus its encoded copy arrays guide T14.2, T37.1 In xarray, set encoding[var] = {chunks, shards, compressors} and rechunk to shard boundaries; never pass safe_chunks=False xarray I/O guide T14.2 The whole-time-axis timeseries preset cannot be appended to: an append rewrites every shard. Append stores use a fixed time chunk (one ministack) and time shards that are whole multiples of it. timeseries stores are frozen snapshots Follows from the sharding and append docs T14.2, T14.2b Default compressor is Zstandard. Benchmark plain zstd against Blosc (zstd with shuffle) for float32 with NaN, and pick from the result (done: Blosc with bit shuffle for float layers, zstd for quality layers in time-spanning chunks) arrays guide, codecs API T37.3b Use only spec-defined codecs from zarr.codecs by default, so GDAL and other readers work. Lossy codecs are opt-in v3 migration T14.2 fill_value is required in v3. NaN for float layers means all-NaN chunks (water, off-frame) are not stored. Set the nodata value of integer masks explicitly; the default is 0 data types T14.2a xarray keeps the CF _FillValue separate from the Zarr fill_value in v3. Round-trip tests check both, and that integer masks do not come back as float xarray I/O guide T14.2a Consolidated metadata is experimental in v3 and not in the spec. Write it for plain stores, re-consolidate after an append, and never require it on read consolidated metadata T14.2 Arrays written with zarr-python directly need dimension_names, or xarray cannot open them xarray Zarr encoding T27.7 async.concurrency defaults to 10 and multiplies with dask threads. Set it through zarr.config or environment variables per job, not in code config guide T37.3a Parallel writers are safe only when they write different chunks (shards, when sharded) performance guide T37.4 FsspecStore is the documented route for object storage; the obstore-backed store is marked experimental storage guide T14.2, T37.3b The multiscales, spatial: and proj: conventions are at version 0.1, pilot maturity, with breaking changes expected. Arbitrary scale factors (33) are allowed. GeoZarr is a suite of these conventions, not yet a finished spec multiscales, spatial, proj, geozarr-spec T27.7 Do not rely on variable (rectilinear) chunking; that ZEP is a draft and xarray rejects it ZEPs T14.2

docs.title: 3. xarray ecosystem
docs.text:
Source: the xarray ecosystem page, every project in every section, plus related projects that are not listed there. Maintenance status was read from GitHub on Oct 1, 2026. Function names for sarxarray, stmtools, xvec, xeofs, flox and xarray-regrid were read from source; the rest comes from project docs. One reader; not independently re-checked.

Nothing InSAR-specific can be a dependency. The two SAR projects work on SLC or point-scatterer data in radar coordinates.

docs.title: 3.1 Dependencies
docs.text: Project Status What disp-xr uses Level Task rioxarray 0.23.0, Jul 2026 CRS and transform. Version 0.23 also writes the Zarr spatial: and proj: conventions; confirm, then let it write them Core T6.2, T14.2a flox 0.11.2, Feb 2026 Grouped reductions (nanmedian, mode, binning). No weighted reductions: a weighted mean is two sums, a weighted median needs disp-xr's own kernel Core T10.3, T23.2, T27.2 numbagg 0.9.6, Sep 2026 Fast NaN-aware reductions and moving windows, picked up by xarray when installed Recommended, not imported T1.5 xvec 0.5.2, Nov 2025; API may change GNSS stations as a vector data cube (station geometry by time), point extraction, GeoDataFrame export gnss extra T25.1 xeofs 3.0.4, Oct 2024; quiet since Jan 2025 EOF, rotated and complex EOF for the gallery. Maintenance risk: core code never imports it, and a CI job reports breakage eof extra T32.6d odc-geo 0.5.3, Jul 2026 Lazy, dask-backed reprojection to a common grid. Evaluate for the mosaic before relying on rio.reproject_match, which loads data Optional, to evaluate T36.1 cf_xarray 0.11.3, Jun 2026 Tests assert that outputs decode as CF test extra T14.5 hvplot with datashader Active Interactive full-frame browsing in one gallery page interactive extra T17.4 xpublish Active Tile serving in the gallery (with xpublish-tiles) Docs only T37.5

docs.title: 3.2 Design references
docs.text:
Nothing from these is imported; disp-xr copies an idea.

Project Idea copied Task SARXarray (1.4.0, Aug 2026) Accessor layout on an SAR stack, and multi_look by coarsen with chosen statistics T9.2, T27.1 H3, matplotlib hexbin, PostGIS ST_HexagonGrid Hexagonal binning: a global hierarchical hexagon grid (H3), and the planar hexagon lattice that hexbin and ST_HexagonGrid build (Carr et al. 1987). They count or average; disp-xr adds quality weights and per-cell sigmas, lazily on the stack. Why hexagons: Birch et al. 2007; global grids: Sahr et al. 2003 T27.8 stmtools (0.1.4) Point data as a (space, time) xarray Dataset with spatial ordering of points for chunk locality; enrichment from polygons and rasters T27.5, T28.4, T25.1 xDEM (0.2.3, Mar 2026) Uncertainty of a spatial average with correlated errors: variogram-based effective sample count (Hugonnet et al. 2022, Rolstad et al. 2009). The simple n_eff = (Σw)² / Σw² ignores spatial correlation and gives cell sigmas that are too small at 1 to 10 km T27.3b, T32.1 xclim (0.62.0) A plain compute function wrapped by one decorator that checks units, sets CF attributes and appends history T9.3 xarray-regrid (0.4.2) nan_threshold semantics for the valid-fraction cutoff of a cell T27.3 xarray-schema Component schemas (dims, dtype, chunks) in validate_disp, including a chunk check T9.5 xproj, rasterix CRS-aware alignment and a raster index built from the affine transform. Too early to depend on; keep grid and CRS access behind one helper so they can be swapped in, and fail on a CRS mismatch (adjacent frames can be in different UTM zones) T9.5, T36.1 xrft (1.0.2) Spectrum scaling and window-correction conventions. Not usable directly: it needs even spacing and no NaNs T22.1, T32.4 xskillscore, xarray-einstats Function signature (a, b, dim, weights, skipna); used as test oracles for RMSE, MAD, skewness and kurtosis T32.1, T32.6b xarray-spatial (0.10.18) IDW, kriging and spline used as cross-checks for disp-xr's own estimators T19.6, T24.4 ndpyramid Pyramid generation; disp-xr writes its own multiscales metadata T27.7

docs.title: 3.3 Checked and not used
docs.text:
• Units: pint-xarray and MetPy's unit handling conflict with the rule that units live in attributes.
  • Regridding: xESMF (ESMF dependency, lat/lon focus), pyinterp.
  • Covered already: geocube, regionmask, salem, GeoWombat, Open Data Cube core (rioxarray and flox cover the need).
  • Fitting: xarray-lmfit (per-pixel lmfit is far too slow for 70 million pixels), eofs (no rotation), X-regression (dead).
  • Catalogs: stackstac, odc-stac, intake-xarray, xstac. DISP discovery goes through CMR.
  • L1 SAR readers: xarray-sentinel, xsar, pyroSAR.
  • Superseded: kerchunk formats (VirtualiZarr recommends Icechunk).
  • After 1.0: TOAD (abrupt-shift detection on (time, y, x) cubes), a candidate when automatic break detection comes into scope.
  • Other domains: the climate, ocean, radar-meteorology, machine-learning and non-Python projects on the page.

docs.title: Finding and reading granules remotely
docs.text: DISP-S1 granules are in NASA's archive at the ASF DAAC. disp-xr finds them through the CMR search API and reads them locally, over HTTPS or directly from S3. The examples on this page need an Earthdata Login and network access, so unlike the gallery they are not run when the docs build.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Put your Earthdata Login in ~/.netrc:

machine urs.earthdata.nasa.gov login YOUR_USER password YOUR_PASSWORD

disp-xr reads it for HTTPS downloads and to request temporary S3 credentials from ASF. The aws extra adds the libraries for remote reads (pip install 'disp_xr[aws]').

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
disp_xr search --frame-id 11116 --start 2024-01-01 --out granules.csv

import disp_xr as dxr

table = dxr.search_granules(frame_id=11116)  # one row per granule, version 1.0
table[["reference_datetime", "secondary_datetime", "generation_datetime", "filename"]]

filename holds the HTTPS URL; url_type="s3" (--url-type s3) gives S3 URLs instead. A frame can have granules from several productions. disp-xr reads productions that differ only in float precision together, with a warning (see the product notes).

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
disp-xr has no download command: any HTTPS client that sends the Earthdata login works. Downloads resume, and six run in parallel:

cut -d, -f9 granules.csv | tail -n +2 > urls.txt
xargs -P 6 -n 1 curl -s -n -L -c .cookies -b .cookies -f -C - -O < urls.txt

docs.title: Read without downloading
docs.text:
open_disp takes a remote prefix or a list of URLs as well as a folder:

import disp_xr as dxr

ds = dxr.open_disp(list(table["filename"]))       # HTTPS, Earthdata login

s3_urls = search(frame_id=11116, url_type="s3")["filename"]
ds = dxr.open_disp(list(s3_urls))                 # S3, in us-west-2

S3 reads use the AWS_* environment variables if set, otherwise temporary ASF credentials (valid one hour, renewed automatically). Direct S3 access works only from AWS us-west-2; elsewhere use HTTPS.

Reading a whole frame over the network is slow: every epoch is a separate file, and opening it reads its metadata. For repeated work, build a virtual frame once. It references the chunks in place, and every later open reads only the chunk index:

dxr.build_virtual_frame(list(s3_urls), "s3://my-bucket/F11116-virtual")
ds = dxr.open_virtual("s3://my-bucket/F11116-virtual")

See the virtual frames example for building, validating and extending one.

docs.title: Static layers
docs.text:
The line-of-sight vectors, DEM and layover/shadow mask come from the frame's DISP-S1-STATIC granule. They are downloaded once and cached:

disp_xr geometry F11116/ --out F11116_static.zarr --static-dir static/

static = dxr.open_static(ds)    # downloads to ~/.cache/disp_xr/static/F11116

Frames outside North America have no DISP-S1-STATIC. Pass your own LOS layers with open_static(ds, files=...).

docs.title: Serving stores over HTTP
docs.text: disp_xr serve exposes stores read-only to web clients: point series, velocities, grid or quadtree cells, GNSS residuals, provenance and map tiles. The REST service gallery page shows every route on a synthetic store. This page covers running it for other people.

docs.title: Prepare the stores
docs.text:
The service reads; it does not process. Give each store what its clients will ask for:

Clients ask for Write into the store Point series (timeseries) The chained cube (disp_xr stack, or to_zarr) Velocities (velocity, cells of velocity) velocity and velocity_sigma from fit_velocity, in the same store GNSS residuals (gnss) residuals.compare(...).to_zarr(store), a gnss group next to the cube Fast point series The timeseries preset (one chunk holds every epoch of a block of pixels) Fast map tiles A GeoZarr pyramid (to_geozarr), served as its own dataset

Full frames are built by region jobs (disp_xr.batch), not by the service.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
pip install "disp_xr[serve]"
disp_xr serve /data/F08882.zarr /data/F11116.zarr --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9000

Each store becomes a dataset named after it (F08882, F11116), served under /datasets/<name>/. The API page is at /docs, the OpenAPI schema at /openapi.json. Stores open lazily: the service reads only the chunks a request needs. Zarr stores, Icechunk repositories and virtual frames (disp_xr virtual) are supported. A virtual frame is chained on open, still lazily, and its reads go to the granules it references, so those must stay where they were when the frame was built.

For more than one worker process, run the application with uvicorn directly, with a small launcher module:

# app.py
from disp_xr.serve import make_app

app = make_app({"F08882": "/data/F08882.zarr"}).app

uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9000 --workers 4

Each worker opens the stores itself. The first request of a worker takes about 0.2 s more than the next ones (pyproj and Zarr warm-up).

docs.title: Behind a reverse proxy
docs.text:
Keep the service on 127.0.0.1 and let a reverse proxy handle TLS, the public path and caching. With nginx, serving the API under /disp-api/:

location /disp-api/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:9000/;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_read_timeout 120s;          # cells on large boxes can take seconds

    # Responses depend only on the URL and the store: cache them.
    proxy_cache disp_api;
    proxy_cache_valid 200 1h;
    add_header X-Cache-Status $upstream_cache_status;

    # Web maps on other origins (the DISP portal) call the API directly.
    add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*" always;
}

with proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx/disp_api keys_zone=disp_api:10m max_size=2g; in the http block. When a store is rebuilt, clear the cache, or put a version in the dataset name (F08882-v2).

The OpenAPI page builds its links from the request, so behind a prefix, start uvicorn with --root-path /disp-api (or pass root_path to the FastAPI application) so /docs works there too.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• cells downsamples at most 4 M pixels per request (413 above), about a 60 x 60 km box of a 30 m frame. Clients should ask for the current map view, not the whole frame.
  • timeseries and velocity take a buffer_m of up to 5 km.
  • There is no authentication: put the proxy's authentication in front if the stores are not public.

docs.title: Try it on your frame
docs.text: This page is for Cal/Val users taking part in the v0.2 API review. It takes about 30 minutes on a frame you know. What we want to learn: does the everyday workflow do what you expect, are the names right, and what is missing? Names can still change before v0.2; after it they are frozen.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/mgovorcin/disp-xr.git
cd disp-xr
pixi install -e dev        # or: pip install -e ".[plot,aws]"

docs.title: 2. Run the workflow on your granules
docs.text:
Use a frame whose behaviour you know (a subsiding city, a stable area, a GNSS site). A few ministacks are enough.

import disp_xr as dxr

table = dxr.find_products("/path/to/your/granules")
print(table.groupby("reference_time").size())   # ministacks as you expect?

ds = dxr.open_disp(table, corrections=True)
ds = ds.disp.correct().disp.mask("recommended").disp.chain()
ds = ds.disp.rereference("point", lon=..., lat=...)   # a point you trust

ds.disp.plot_map()
ds.disp.plot_point(lon=..., lat=...)            # a place you know
dxr.to_zarr(ds, "my_frame.zarr")

Or the same from the command line:

disp_xr info /path/to/your/granules
disp_xr stack /path/to/your/granules --out my_frame.zarr --reference point --lon ... --lat ...
disp_xr export my_frame.zarr --format cog --out last.tif

docs.title: 3. Tell us
docs.text:
Open an issue on the repository (or reply to the review email) with:

  1. Frame and data: frame id, number of granules, product version, where they were stored (local disk, S3).
  2. What worked and what did not: errors, wrong-looking results, steps that were slow (with times), anything you had to look up.
  3. Names and defaults: anything you would call differently. The open questions are listed in the API review; a short answer to each helps.
  4. What is missing for your Cal/Val work.

Thank you. Feedback is triaged into one issue per topic, and the agreed changes are applied before v0.2 is tagged.

docs.title: Choosing a velocity method
docs.text:
disp-xr has four ways to estimate a velocity. They differ in how they treat noise, how fast they are, and how long a record they need. The short answer:

Your case Use Exact colored-noise sigmas for every pixel, any length from about 60 epochs fit_velocity(ds, "gls") Full DISP-S1 record, 200 epochs or more (about 6.5 years at 12 days), fastest fit_velocity(ds, "whittle") One pixel or station, to study its noise fit_noise (exact); consider FNWN for the shortest records Unmodelled steps, outliers or unwrapping jumps, several years of data fit_velocity(ds, "midas") as a robust check A quick map, or comparing pixels with each other fit_velocity(ds, "ols"), but do not use its sigma

The rest of this page explains why.

docs.title: The methods
docs.text: Method Velocity Sigma Noise model Cost fit_velocity(ds, "ols") least squares with your Trajectory white noise only none fast, every pixel fit_velocity(ds, "whittle") the same least-squares velocity colored noise, per pixel power law plus white (PLWN), estimated per pixel moderate, every pixel fit_velocity(ds, "midas") median of one-year slopes, outliers trimmed MIDAS, deliberately conservative none (empirical) fast, every pixel fit_velocity(ds, "gls") generalized least squares colored noise, exact, per pixel shape (kappa, white fraction) per group of pixels, by exact maximum likelihood on a sample; amplitude per pixel exact fits of the samples, then about 1 s per 256 x 256 tile fit_noise(times, y, model=...) generalized least squares colored noise, exact WN, FNWN, PLWN or RWFNWN 0.1 to 1 s per series (n x n covariance)

docs.title: Why not OLS sigmas
docs.text: InSAR and GNSS noise is correlated in time (flicker-like, kappa near -1). Least squares treats every epoch as independent, so its sigma is too small. On the test series in tests/data/noise_reference.json the white-noise sigma is 3 to 30 times smaller than the colored-noise sigma of the same data. The OLS velocity itself is fine; only its uncertainty is wrong.

docs.title: Record length: where the 200 comes from
docs.text:
The limit applies to Whittle only. Whittle estimates the noise from the periodogram, an approximation that becomes exact as the record grows. benchmarks/whittle_bias.py compared it with the exact estimate on 30 simulated 12-day series per length (trend, flicker with kappa -1, white noise):

Epochs Years kappa, exact kappa, Whittle Velocity error / sigma, exact Same, Whittle 60 2.0 -1.03 -0.19 1.06 1.86 100 3.3 -0.92 -0.75 1.21 1.47 200 6.6 -0.94 -0.81 0.94 1.01 400 13.1 -1.04 -1.00 0.84 0.81

A ratio near 1 in the last two columns means the sigma is honest; above 1 it is too small. From about 200 epochs Whittle is as good as the exact estimate; at 100 its sigmas are about 1.5 times too small, at 60 nearly 2 times. fit_velocity(method="whittle") logs a warning below 200 epochs.

The exact estimate (fit_noise) stays calibrated down to 60 epochs, but it costs a factorization of an n x n matrix per likelihood evaluation, so it is for single pixels, GNSS stations or small groups. fit_velocity(ds, "gls") brings it to whole frames: it fits a sample of each group's pixels exactly to get the group's noise shape, then solves every pixel by exact GLS with that shape and its own amplitude, so it inherits the exact estimate's behaviour on short records.

docs.title: Groups for "gls"
docs.text: Pixels with similar noise should share a group. By default they are binned by time-mean temporal_coherence (n_groups quantile bins); you can pass any integer map (y, x) instead, for example regions you trust or, later, quadtree cells. More samples per group (n_samples, default 16) steady the shape estimate at the cost of more exact fits. Check attrs["noise_groups"] for each group's model, kappa and white fraction.

docs.title: Which noise model (fit_noise)
docs.text:
Model Noise When PLWN power law with free kappa, plus white the default FNWN flicker (kappa fixed at -1) plus white the standard GNSS model; one parameter fewer, so steadier on short records where kappa is poorly constrained (a judgment, not measured here: the study above fitted PLWN only) RWFNWN random walk, flicker and white long records with suspected random-walk drift (monument motion, slowly accumulating unwrapping errors) WN white only testing; equivalent to OLS

When unsure, fit several and compare res.bic (lower is better): BIC penalizes extra noise parameters, so it prefers FNWN unless the data support a free kappa or a random walk. fit_velocity(method="whittle") always uses PLWN; method="gls" takes noise= with any of these, or noise="auto" to choose FNWN, PLWN or RWFNWN per group by the median BIC of its samples.

docs.title: When MIDAS
docs.text:
MIDAS takes the median of slopes between epochs about one year apart (Blewitt et al., 2016). Steps, outliers and seasonal signals affect only some pairs, so it needs no step dates and no seasonal terms. Use it:

  • as a check on a trajectory fit, where a large difference points to a step or outlier the model misses;
  • when steps are not known in advance (unwrapping jumps, equipment or processing changes).

It needs a record of several years: every pair spans a year, and a step biases the median when the pairs that cross it are a large share, about one year divided by the record length. On a 3-year synthetic record with a 10 mm step the bias was clear; on 6 years it was small. Its sigma is deliberately conservative (an empirical factor of 3 makes it realistic for colored noise), so it is often larger than the Whittle sigma for the same pixel.

docs.title: Model what you know
docs.text: OLS and Whittle fit the Trajectory you give them. Include known steps (earthquakes, reference changes not handled by chaining) and the seasonal terms; an unmodelled step or seasonal cycle ends up in the residuals and inflates the estimated noise. Whittle estimates the noise from those residuals, so a missing term also makes its sigma too large.

docs.title: batch
docs.text:
Build a frame cube with independent region jobs (PRD C6, plan task T37.4).

Modeled on earth-mover's serverless-datacube-demo. A coordinator:

  1. builds a lazy template of the output (for example dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp(granules))), which reads no pixel;
  2. writes the store's metadata once with :func:init_store;
  3. splits the frame into regions aligned to the shards with :func:plan_jobs; each :class:RegionJob serializes to JSON, one per AWS Batch array index or dask task;

and each worker runs :func:run_region: it opens the granules on its region, applies a processing function, overwrites its own shards and returns a :class:RegionResult. Shards are the unit of safe parallel writing, and a job owns whole shards, so a retry overwrites them cleanly. The results form a manifest, and :func:failed_jobs lists the jobs to resubmit.

The granule list is resolved once by the coordinator and travels in the jobs. Workers reading s3:// granules get temporary ASF credentials, cached and renewed after 50 minutes, so each job starts with valid ones.

Processing must be local in space: masking, corrections, chaining and per-pixel fits work region by region; a spatial reference or a deramp needs the whole frame, so apply it after the cube is assembled (lazily, on the store).

Examples:

>>> template = dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp(granules))
>>> shards = init_store(template, "frame.zarr")
>>> jobs = plan_jobs(template, "frame.zarr", granules, shards)
>>> results = [run_region(job, chain) for job in jobs]
>>> retry = failed_jobs(jobs, results)

Examples:

>>> job = RegionJob(

...     region={"y": [0, 1024], "x": [0, 1024]},
...     granules=["g1.nc", "g2.nc"],
... )
>>> RegionJob.from_json(job.to_json()) == job
True
>>> job.slices["y"]
slice(0, 1024, None)

docs.title: Icechunk and virtual stores
docs.text:
These need the cloud extra (pip install "disp_xr[cloud]").

Write and read DISP datasets in Icechunk repositories (cloud extra).

An Icechunk repository is a versioned Zarr v3 store: every write is a commit with a snapshot id, and tags name snapshots that must not move (a Cal/Val run). to_icechunk wraps :func:icechunk.xarray.to_icechunk, which, unlike ds.to_zarr on a session store, keeps writes made under dask.distributed or multiprocessing.

Provenance (disp-xr and package versions, product, frame, input granules and the history of operations) goes in the commit metadata as well as in the dataset attributes. A stack built by appending one ministack per commit uses the "ministack" chunk preset, so an append writes new shards instead of rewriting old ones. Library code never amends a commit or expires snapshots.

docs.title: to_icechunk
docs.text:
to_icechunk(ds: Dataset, repo: RepoLike, *, branch: str = 'main', message: Optional[str] = None, append_dim: Optional[str] = None, tag: Optional[str] = None, preset: Optional[Preset] = None, mode: Literal['w-', 'w'] = 'w-', keep_bits: Optional[int] = None, compression_level: int = 3, target_mb: Optional[float] = None) -> str

Write ds to an Icechunk repository as one commit.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ds Dataset

DISP dataset with (time, y, x) and (y, x) variables.

required repo (Repository, str or Path)

Repository, or a local directory (created if missing).

required branch str

Branch to commit to. A missing branch is created from main.

'main' message str

Commit message; defaults to a summary of the write.

None append_dim 'time'

Append along time. The dataset must be on the store's grid, with the same variables and dtypes, and start after the store's last epoch. On an empty branch this creates the store with the "ministack" layout.

"time" tag str

Tag the new snapshot (for example a Cal/Val run). Tags never move.

None preset ('timeseries', 'maps', 'ministack')

Chunk layout of a new store; ignored when appending to an existing one. Defaults to "timeseries", or "ministack" with append_dim. "timeseries" cannot be appended to, since each shard spans the whole time axis and every append would rewrite it.

"timeseries" mode ('w-', 'w')

Without append_dim: fail if the branch has data (default), or replace it in a new commit (older snapshots stay readable).

"w-" keep_bits Optional[int]

As in :func:disp_xr.to_zarr.

None compression_level Optional[int]

As in :func:disp_xr.to_zarr.

None target_mb Optional[int]

As in :func:disp_xr.to_zarr.

None

docs.title: Virtual stores
docs.text:
Virtual DISP frames: Icechunk stores that point at the granules (cloud extra).

A virtual store holds no pixels. Each layer chunk is a reference to a byte range in a granule, read through VirtualiZarr's HDF parser, so a whole frame opens as one Zarr dataset without copying data. time, reference_time, x, y and spatial_ref are loaded into the store, because their encoding differs between granules; the /identification and /metadata groups are not read.

Displacement stays relative to each ministack reference, as in the granules: chain and re-reference on top of :func:open_virtual. A virtual store is an index for ingest and exploration; for per-pixel work write a native store (:func:disp_xr.to_zarr with the "timeseries" preset).

The store registers a virtual chunk container for the granule location (the S3 bucket, or the local directory). Credentials for it are given when the repository is opened and are never saved with it.

Write a frame of granules to an Icechunk repository as virtual references.

One commit per ministack, in reference-date order. A branch that already holds a frame is extended: every new ministack must start after its last epoch and be on the same grid, with the same layers and dtypes.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default granules str, Path, iterable of paths, or DataFrame

Local or s3:// granules of one frame and one production, or the output of :func:disp_xr.find_products.

required repo (Repository, Storage, str or Path)

Repository to write to. For a storage or a local path, the repository is created if needed and a virtual chunk container for the granule location is registered. A Repository must already have one and be opened with access to it.

required branch str

Branch to commit to.

'main' layers sequence of str

Layers to reference. Defaults to all displacement and quality layers.

None max_workers int

Processes that parse granules; 1 parses in this process.

None credentials AWSCredentials

For s3:// granules. Defaults to AWS_* environment variables, then ASF temporary credentials.

None

Returns:

Type Description list of str

Snapshot id of each commit, one per ministack.

Raises:

If the granules mix productions (dtype or encoding differ).

Examples:

>>> snapshots = dxr.build_virtual_frame(
...     "F11116/", "F11116-virtual/"
... )

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
disp_xr.config holds the runtime settings. Change them for a block of code with config.set, or for a batch job with DISP_XR_* environment variables (nested keys use a double underscore).

from disp_xr.config import config

with config.set({"chunks.target_mb": 50}):
    ...
Key Default Meaning chunks.target_mb 100 Uncompressed size of one dask chunk (and Zarr shard) for the timeseries and maps presets, in MB chunks.read_block 1024 Spatial block read from each granule; the native chunk size max_load_bytes 2 GiB Largest array export and plotting load into memory cache.dir None Downloaded static layers; None means $XDG_CACHE_HOME/disp_xr or ~/.cache/disp_xr threads None Threads per worker for compiled kernels num_workers 32 Dask threads when disp-xr computes (plots, exports), unless dask's own num_workers is set numba_threads 1 Threads of numba kernels (numbagg) inside each dask task, set as NUMBA_NUM_THREADS on import unless that variable is set or numba is already loaded; numba's default of one per core made every dask thread open 224 threads on a large node and crash

docs.title: Chunks
docs.text:
Dask chunk sizes for DISP stacks.

Chunks are sized from a byte target (config["chunks.target_mb"]), not a fixed shape, and aligned to the 256 x 256 HDF5 chunks of DISP granules so a dask chunk never reads part of a file chunk. Three presets:

"native" (the :func:disp_xr.open_disp default) One epoch and one read block (config["chunks.read_block"], 1,024 x 1,024) per chunk: the layout of the files. Every selection reads only the epochs and blocks it needs, so maps, points and chaining stay cheap. "timeseries" The whole time axis in each chunk, for per-pixel work (fits, filters). Functions that need it rechunk to it themselves (:func:time_contiguous, which merges time within the input's spatial blocks instead of reshuffling them). "maps" One epoch per chunk, sized to the byte target, for whole-map work.

:func:rechunk switches a dataset between them when one kind of access will be repeated, for example ds.disp.rechunk("timeseries") before many point reads of a store that fits in memory.

Clamping is adapted from opera-utils (src/opera_utils/disp/_utils.py, _clamp_chunk_dict, commit 97f77d9), Copyright (c) 2022 California Institute of Technology, BSD-3-Clause. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

rechunk(obj: Any, chunks: Optional[ChunkSpec] = None) -> Any

Return obj (Dataset or DataArray) with dask chunks for one kind of work.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default obj Dataset or DataArray

DISP data with time, y, x dimensions (any subset).

required chunks ('native', 'timeseries', 'maps')

A preset (see the module docstring) or explicit {"time", "y", "x"} sizes, -1 for a whole axis. Required: leaving it out still means "timeseries" but warns, and is an error from 1.0 (so every call says which layout it asks for).

>>> rechunk(da, "timeseries").chunks[0]
(4,)

docs.title: GeoZarr for bowser
docs.text:
GeoZarr stores that bowser opens directly (PRD C4, plan task T27.9).

to_geozarr(ds, store) writes a GeoZarr store: the multiscale pyramid of :func:disp_xr.to_pyramid (or one flat group), with CF and Zarr proj: / spatial: metadata on every level. profile="bowser" (the default) adds what bowser <https://github.com/opera-adt/bowser>_ uses to display the data, without changing anything a strict GeoZarr reader relies on:

  • display levels by factor 2 until the shorter side is under 256 cells (bowser picks the level whose pixel matches the tile pixel, so analysis factors such as 33 alone leave mid zooms reading 30 m);
  • bowser_uses_spatial_ref on every variable: true only for displacement and velocity. Otherwise bowser infers it from the units and subtracts a reference value from sigmas (meters) and inversion residuals (radians);
  • long_name on every variable (the colorbar title);
  • reference_lonlat from :func:disp_xr.rereference (a point reference), shown as the reference marker;
  • the line-of-sight attributes bowser reads (heading_angle_deg, incidence_angle_deg and los_enu_ground_to_satellite, near, center and far) from the static layers, when given;
  • bowser_histogram per epoch on level 0 (bins and percentiles), so the histogram panel does not read a full-resolution epoch per request;
  • float32 data, and chunks of one epoch by 256 x 256 in shards of 4 epochs by 1,024 x 1,024 (the "tiles" preset, bowser's tuned layout).

Checked against bowser ops (0a61c6a; zarr 3.1.1, xarray 2025.8, rioxarray 0.19) with tests/bowser_check.py: the per-level proj: and spatial: attributes, the multiscales transform, consolidated metadata, spatial_ref as a coordinate, integer masks with a _FillValue (decoded to NaN) and one-chunk small levels do not change what bowser reads or shows.

docs.title: Multiscale pyramids
docs.text:
Multiscale pyramids of downsampled levels in Zarr (PRD C4, plan task T27.7).

A pyramid is one Zarr group whose children are the levels, as sibling groups 0 (the input, 30 m), 1, 2, ... (each from :func:disp_xr.downsample of level 0). Every level is self-contained: CF spatial_ref, the Zarr proj: and spatial: attributes with its own spatial:transform and spatial:shape, and the provenance attributes. The root carries the multiscales layout: per level its asset, derived_from, the relative transform (scale = factor, translation 0, since cell edges start at the first pixel edge), the absolute spatial:transform and spatial:shape, the resampling method, and the reduction of each variable under disp_xr:resampling.

The multiscales, spatial: and proj: conventions are at pilot maturity (multiscales v0.1, breaking changes expected before v1), so their ids and URLs live only in this module and the version is recorded in the root attributes. :func:open_pyramid finds levels from the layout, never from group names.

Conventions: https://github.com/zarr-conventions/multiscales (v0.1), https://github.com/zarr-conventions/spatial, https://github.com/zarr-conventions/proj.

docs.title: GNSS
docs.text:
GNSS stations next to DISP, with geepers as the engine (install the gnss extra). geepers loads, caches and reads the station series; disp_xr.gnss returns them as xarray and aligns them with DISP.

gps = dxr.gnss.load(ds, start="2017-01-01")            # (station, time) E/N/U
gps = dxr.gnss.to_los(gps, dxr.open_static(ds))        # + los, sigma_los
insar = dxr.gnss.sample(ds, gps, buffer_m=100)         # DISP at the stations
gps_on_disp = dxr.gnss.align(gps["los"], insar.time)   # DISP epochs and reference
residual = insar - gps_on_disp

GNSS stations next to DISP, with geepers as the engine (PRD F10, task T25).

geepers (https://github.com/opera-adt/geepers, the gnss extra) loads the GNSS series: its sources (UNR, UNR grid, sideshow) download, cache and read station files, and its sampler reads DISP around each station. This module adapts them to xarray and to DISP:

  • :func:get_source picks a geepers source; :func:stations lists the stations over a frame;
  • :func:load returns a (station, time) Dataset of east, north and up motion with sigmas and correlations, and station coordinates in lon/lat and in the frame's CRS;
  • :func:to_los projects them onto the line of sight with the static layers (sigma from geepers get_sigma_los);
  • :func:sample reads DISP at the stations (median in a window, geepers sample_insar);
  • :func:align puts GNSS on the DISP epochs and on the DISP reference date.
  • :func:centred stamps daily solutions at the centre of their UTC day.
  • :func:drop_relocations keeps each station's longest record between monument moves (applied by :func:load).

Typical use::

gps = dxr.gnss.load(ds, start="2017-01-01")
gps_los = dxr.gnss.to_los(gps, dxr.open_static(ds))
insar = dxr.gnss.sample(ds, gps, buffer_m=100)
gps_aligned = dxr.gnss.align(gps_los["los"], insar.time)

None end str
