None max_workers int

8 max_step_m float or None

A larger one is not ground motion (near-field coseismic steps reach about 5 m) but a monument moved under the same id: the record is split there and only the segment with the most solutions is kept (:func:drop_relocations). With buffer_m, geepers releases that have buffer_meters take a circular window of that radius; older ones (0.3) a square window of the same half-width in pixels.

docs.text:
align(gnss: DataArray, times: Union[DataArray, DatetimeIndex, ndarray], *, reference: Optional[Any] = None, method: Literal['nearest', 'linear'] = 'nearest', tolerance: str = '1D') -> xr.DataArray

Put a GNSS series on the DISP epochs and the DISP reference date.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default gnss DataArray

(station, time) GNSS series, for example to_los(...)["los"].

required times array of datetimes

DISP epochs (ds.time).

required reference date - like

DISP reference date; default the first epoch (a chained stack is relative to it).

None method ('nearest', 'linear')

Nearest GNSS solution within tolerance, or linear interpolation. Daily solutions count as stamped at noon (:func:centred), so an epoch takes the solution of its own UTC day.

"nearest" tolerance str

Largest distance in time for "nearest" (pandas offset).

'1D'

Returns:

Type Description DataArray

GNSS at times minus its value at reference; NaN where the GNSS series does not reach an epoch. A station with no solution at reference (installed later, or a gap that day) is referenced to its first epoch instead, so its residual against DISP carries a constant offset, which rates and mean-removed statistics ignore. The gnss_reference coordinate gives each station's reference epoch.

Examples:

>>> on_epochs = dxr.gnss.align(los["los"], ds.time)

docs.title: DISP against GNSS
docs.text:
dxr.residuals.compare reads DISP at the stations (or the downsampled cell holding each one), puts GNSS on the DISP epochs and reference, and lets geepers compute the metrics.

result = dxr.residuals.compare(ds, gps, static, buffer_m=100,
                               requirement=lambda d: (3 + 0.5 * d**0.5) / 1000)
result.stations          # velocities, normalized residuals, chi2, outliers
result.profile           # pairwise RMSE against distance, with the requirement
result.plot_velocities()

An EOF analysis of trajectory residuals with xeofs (eof extra) is in examples/eof_residuals.py; it runs in its own CI job.

docs.title: compare
docs.text:
compare(data: Any, gnss: Dataset, static: Dataset, *, buffer_m: float = 0.0, layer: str = 'displacement', velocity_method: str = 'lsq', tolerance: str = '1D', min_common_dates: int = 3, min_stations: int = 3, min_epochs: int = 10, min_span_years: float = 2.0, n_bins: int = 10, requirement: Optional[Any] = DISP_S1_DISPLACEMENT, velocity_requirement: Optional[Requirement] = DISP_S1_VELOCITY, outlier_sigma: float = 3.0, epoch_flag: float = 3.0, disp_sigma: Optional[float] = None) -> Comparison

Compare DISP with GNSS at the stations (or the cells holding them).

geepers computes the metrics (velocities from one estimator applied to both series, pairwise differential RMSE against distance, its binned profile and semivariogram, epoch RMSE, agreement statistics); disp-xr prepares the series and adds normalized velocity residuals, reduced χ² per station and flags.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data xr.Dataset, point table or Quadtree

DISP at 30 m (read at each station with :func:disp_xr.gnss.sample), or downsampled cells: a point table from :func:disp_xr.to_points or :func:disp_xr.downsample_hex (the nearest cell center) or a :class:disp_xr.Quadtree (the leaf holding the station).

required gnss Dataset

:func:disp_xr.gnss.load output for the same frame.

required static Dataset

LOS layers for :func:disp_xr.gnss.to_los.

required buffer_m float

Window radius for sampling 30 m data.

0.0 layer str

DISP layer.

'displacement' velocity_method ('lsq', 'midas', 'trend')

Estimator for both series (geepers fit_velocities); MIDAS needs about a year of data.

"lsq" tolerance str

Largest gap between a DISP epoch and a GNSS day.

'1D' min_common_dates int

Passed to geepers (pairs, epochs, profile).

3 min_stations int

Passed to geepers (pairs, epochs, profile).

3 n_bins int

Passed to geepers (pairs, epochs, profile).

3 min_epochs int

Least number of epochs with both series, and least time between the first and last of them, for a station's velocities to count. A rate from a few epochs says nothing about the product, yet it would enter the velocity residuals, the outlier flag and the GNSS tie. Below either, the velocities and their sigmas are NaN and velocity_usable is False; the station's displacement series still enters the pairs and the epoch RMSE.

10 min_span_years int

Least number of epochs with both series, and least time between the first and last of them, for a station's velocities to count. A rate from a few epochs says nothing about the product, yet it would enter the velocity residuals, the outlier flag and the GNSS tie. Below either, the velocities and their sigmas are NaN and velocity_usable is False; the station's displacement series still enters the pairs and the epoch RMSE.

10 requirement Requirement or callable

Threshold of the pairwise relative displacement RMSE against distance, drawn on the profile with geepers' fraction_passing. Default :data:DISP_S1_DISPLACEMENT. A :class:Requirement follows the units of layer; a plain requirement(distance_km) must return the units of the data. None for no requirement.

DISP_S1_DISPLACEMENT velocity_requirement Requirement

Threshold of the relative velocity: every station pair's difference of velocity residuals is scored against it (velocity_pairs, summary["velocity_fraction_passing"] over the pairs inside its distance range). Default :data:DISP_S1_VELOCITY; None to skip.

DISP_S1_VELOCITY outlier_sigma float

Stations with |normalized_residual| or sqrt(chi2) above this are flagged.

3.0 disp_sigma float

Noise of one DISP epoch at a station, in the units of layer, added in quadrature to the GNSS sigma in chi2. Default: estimated from all stations' residuals (1.4826 MAD, less the median GNSS variance), so one bad station does not raise it.

None epoch_flag float

Epochs whose RMSE exceeds the median plus this many MADs are flagged.

3.0

Returns:

Type Description Comparison

Examples:

>>> gps = dxr.gnss.load(ds)
>>> result = compare(ds, gps, dxr.open_static(ds))
>>> result.stations[["velocity_residual", "outlier"]]
>>> cells = compare(dxr.quadtree(ds, n_points=5000), gps, static)

docs.title: Spatial models
docs.text:
Estimators with a fit / predict interface for spatial models: trends, the GNSS tie (T33) will build on them. verde is the design reference, not a dependency.

from disp_xr import models

flat = ds.disp.deramp(degree=1)  # a plane removed from every epoch, lazily

coords = models.coordinates(points)  # (easting, northing) of a point table
est = models.Chain([("trend", models.Trend(1)), ("spline", models.Spline(1e-6))])
est.fit(coords, points.velocity.values)
grid = est.grid(like=ds)  # on the frame's grid, with its CRS
scores = models.cross_val_score(est, coords, points.velocity.values, spacing=5000)

Estimator base for spatial models (PRD F9, plan task T19).

Spatial models (trends, GNSS ties, gridders) share one shape, after verde (the design reference only, not a dependency; PRD decision):

  • fit(coords, data, weights=None) estimates the parameters and returns the estimator; fitted attributes end in _;
  • predict(coords) evaluates the model at any coordinates;
  • score(coords, data, weights=None) is the weighted R²;
  • grid(...) predicts on a regular grid as an xr.DataArray with a CRS;
  • :class:Chain fits steps in sequence, each on the residual of the last.

Coordinates are a tuple (easting, northing) of arrays of one shape, in the CRS of the data (projected, in meters for DISP frames). :func:coordinates builds them from a raster, a point table or a DataFrame. :func:cross_val_score scores an estimator with spatial block k-fold cross-validation, which keeps neighbors out of each other's folds (Roberts et al. 2017, https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881).

docs.title: BaseEstimator
docs.text:
Base class of disp-xr spatial estimators.

Subclasses take their parameters as keyword arguments of __init__ (stored under the same names) and implement _fit(easting, northing, data, weights) and _predict(easting, northing) on 1D arrays without NaN; the base class checks inputs, drops NaN and reshapes.

Examples:

>>> class Offset(BaseEstimator):
...     def fit(self, coords, data, weights=None): ...
...     def predict(self, coords): ...

docs.title: Trends and de-ramping
docs.text:
Polynomial trends and per-epoch de-ramping (PRD F9, plan task T24).

:class:Trend fits a 2D polynomial of the coordinates by weighted least squares, on coordinates centered and scaled for conditioning (the raw UTM values, near 10⁶, would make the normal matrix singular in float64 from degree 2). It is the simplest spatial model and a step of the GNSS tie.

:func:deramp removes a polynomial ramp from every epoch of a stack. In the temporal-denoising study, per-epoch spatial de-ramping cut velocity scatter by 10 to 24%, more than any temporal filter. The fit only needs sums over pixels (the normal equations), so it stays lazy and exact; it runs on every stride-th pixel by default and the ramp is subtracted from the full grid chunk by chunk. Ramps are long-wavelength by construction: remove them only when long-wavelength signal (plate motion, large subsidence bowls) is not wanted, or mask such areas out of the fit.

docs.title: Gridders
docs.text:
Gridders for point data (PRD F9, plan task T24.4).

:class:Spline is the biharmonic spline of Sandwell (1987, https://doi.org/10.1029/GL014i002p00139): the field is a sum of Green's functions g(r) = r² (ln r - 1) centered on the data points, with forces from weighted least squares and optional damping (verde's Spline is the design reference, not a dependency). It suits smooth fields from scattered points (GNSS velocities, downsampled cells). The system is dense, n x n for n points, so keep n to a few thousand (downsample first).

:class:Nearest copies the value of the nearest point with positive weight: a fallback with no smoothing.

docs.title: GNSS tie
docs.text:
GNSS tie: remove long-wavelength DISP error with GNSS (PRD F9, plan task T33).

The residual DISP minus GNSS at the stations is fitted with a smooth surface (a polynomial trend, optionally plus a damped spline) and the predicted field is subtracted from DISP, either for the velocity or for every epoch.

What the tie field may hold. Only long-wavelength error: orbits, long-wavelength troposphere and ionosphere, reference-frame and plate-motion differences. Local deformation (groundwater subsidence, coseismic steps) must stay in the calibrated product, so stations in deforming areas are left out of the fit (exclude) and their signal is restored by construction: the smooth field does not reach it. A plane (degree=1) is the default; add the spline only with damping strong enough that its scale stays well above the station spacing. Leave-one-station-out scores improve as the field gets more local, partly by construction (a field that bends to each station predicts its neighbors well), so a better score alone does not show that the signal was preserved.

docs.title: fit_tie
docs.text:
fit_tie(comparison: Any, *, mode: Mode = 'velocity', degree: int = 1, damping: Optional[float] = None, exclude: Any = None) -> TieResult

Fit a GNSS tie to the DISP-minus-GNSS residual at the stations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default comparison Comparison

:func:disp_xr.residuals.compare output.

required mode ('velocity', 'epoch')

Fit the velocity residual (insar_velocity - gps_velocity, weights 1 / velocity_sigma²) or the displacement residual of every epoch (weights 1 / sigma_gnss²).

"velocity" degree int

:class:GNSSTie parameters.

1 damping int

:class:GNSSTie parameters.

1 exclude list of station ids, or a lon/lat polygon

Stations left out of the fit, for example those in deforming areas (subsidence, coseismic): their signal must stay in the product.

None

Returns:

Type Description TieResult

Examples:

>>> comparison = dxr.residuals.compare(ds, gps, static)
>>> tie = fit_tie(comparison, mode="velocity")
>>> tie = fit_tie(comparison, exclude=["P539"])

docs.title: apply_tie
docs.text:
apply_tie(ds: Dataset, tie: TieResult, *, layer: str = 'displacement') -> xr.Dataset

Subtract a GNSS tie from layer.

Epoch mode subtracts each epoch's correction (zero where no tie was fitted). Velocity mode subtracts the correction from a velocity layer, or from displacement as the corrected rate times the time since the first epoch.

Examples:

>>> corrected = apply_tie(ds, tie)

docs.title: cross_validate_tie
docs.text:
cross_validate_tie(comparison: Any, *, mode: Mode = 'velocity', degree: int = 1, damping: Optional[float] = None, exclude: Any = None) -> pd.DataFrame

Leave-one-station-out: residual RMSE at each station before and after.

Each station used in the fit is left out in turn, the tie is fitted on the others and predicted at it. Excluded stations are scored with the tie of all used stations (they never enter the fit).

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

Per station: rmse_before (of its residual) and rmse_after (after subtracting the prediction), excluded; attrs holds the network RMSE before and after (rmse_*), and the median of the per-station values (median_*). The RMSE is driven by single stations (local subsidence, a short record); the median describes the typical station.

Examples:

>>> scores = cross_validate_tie(comparison, mode="epoch")
>>> scores.attrs["rmse_before"], scores.attrs["rmse_after"]
>>> scores.attrs["median_before"], scores.attrs["median_after"]

cross_val_score(estimator: BaseEstimator, coords: Coords, data: Any, *, spacing: float, weights: Optional[Any] = None, n_splits: int = 5, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray

docs.text:
open_disp(paths: PathsLike, *, layers: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None, corrections: bool = False, chunks: ChunkSpec = 'native', frame_id: Optional[int] = None, min_version: Optional[str] = None, check: bool = True) -> xr.Dataset

Open DISP granules of one frame as a lazy dataset.

Displacement is returned as stored: relative to each granule's reference date (reference_time). Chaining across ministacks is a separate step.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default paths str, Path, iterable of paths, or DataFrame

A directory, files, or the output of :func:disp_xr.product.find_products.

required layers sequence of str

Layers to keep. Defaults to all displacement and quality layers.

None corrections bool

Also open the /corrections group layers.

False chunks ('native', 'timeseries', 'maps')

Dask chunks. "native" (default) keeps the file layout, one epoch and one read block per chunk, so any selection reads only what it needs; functions that work along time rechunk for themselves. "timeseries" and "maps" are sized from config["chunks.target_mb"]; a dict gives {"time", "y", "x"} sizes (-1 means the whole axis). See :func:disp_xr.rechunk.

"native" frame_id int

Frame to keep when paths holds several.

None min_version str

Lowest product version to keep.

None check bool

Refuse granules of mixed productions (see :func:disp_xr.product.check_granules). Productions that differ only in the precision of a float layer (DISP-S1 displacement is float32 before November 2025 and float64 after) are read together with a :class:~disp_xr.product.MixedPrecisionWarning; those layers are cast to float32 and listed in attrs["mixed_precision"].

True

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

Dims (time, y, x); coordinates time, reference_time, x, y and spatial_ref (times to the second, as in granule names); one variable per layer, each with grid_mapping. No pixel is read until computed. Layers keep their stored dtype: float layers use NaN for no data, integer layers (masks, labels, counts) keep the product's nodata value, given in their _FillValue attribute.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a requested layer does not exist in the product.

Examples:

>>> ds = dxr.open_disp("F11116/")
>>> ds = dxr.open_disp(
...     "F11116/", layers=["displacement", "temporal_coherence"]
... )
>>> ds = dxr.open_disp(list(search_table["filename"]))

docs.title: Plot
docs.text:
These need the plot extra (pip install "disp_xr[plot]"). The functions live in disp_xr.plot and are methods of the accessor: ds.disp.plot_map(), ds.disp.plot_point(lon, lat).

Quick-look maps and point time series (plot extra).

Plotting is one of the two places disp-xr computes (with export): a map loads one epoch, a point loads one pixel series. Both convert lengths to units (millimeters by default) and label the axes with them.

Displacement is signed (positive toward the satellite), so maps use a diverging blue-gray-red scale centered on zero, with limits symmetric about it. Point plots draw a dashed rule at every reference-date change, where a chained series is joined or an unchained one restarts at zero.

Each epoch loses v_los * (time - reference), where the reference is the granule's reference_time before :func:disp_xr.chain and attrs["reference_date"] after it, so it works on either. The result is in a plate-fixed frame, comparable with plate-fixed GNSS.

Only displacement and short_wavelength_displacement are masked; quality layers are kept as they are. See :func:valid_mask for presets and criteria. Every layer is per epoch, so each epoch is masked by its own granule's quality. Works before or after chaining; the zero epoch that :func:disp_xr.chain prepends has no quality layers and stays 0.

Presets: "recommended" uses the product's recommended_mask; "strict" adds connected components, water and temporal_coherence >= the threshold stored on recommended_mask (0.6 if absent). Keyword arguments add to or override the preset; False turns a criterion off. A pixel at an integer layer's no-data value fails.

docs.text:
quality_summary(ds: Dataset, *, reliability_threshold: float = 0.9, by_ministack: bool = False) -> xr.Dataset

Summarize quality per pixel over time (lazy).

Percentages divide by the epochs where the layer has data, so a stacked zero epoch or missing granules do not count as bad.

Returns:

pct_masked (% of epochs with recommended_mask == 0), pct_ps (% of epochs flagged persistent scatterer), temporal_coherence_hmean (harmonic mean, which down-weights low coherence periods), reliability (fraction of epochs with recommended_mask == 1) and reliable (reliability >= reliability_threshold). docs.title: quality_weights
docs.text:
quality_weights(ds: Dataset, layers: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_LAYERS, *, exponents: Optional[Mapping[str, float]] = None, floors: Optional[Mapping[str, float]] = None, penalty: float = 0.5, f0: float = 0.25, min_residual: float = 0.05) -> xr.Dataset

Combine quality layers into pixel weights between 0 and 1.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ds Dataset

DISP data with the chosen layers (as from :func:disp_xr.open_disp), chained or not.

required layers sequence of str

Any of phase_similarity, temporal_coherence, timeseries_inversion_residuals.

DEFAULT_LAYERS exponents mapping

Relative weight of each layer in the geometric mean (default 1 each).

None floors mapping

Stretch floor per similarity or coherence layer. Default: the processor's thresholds recorded on recommended_mask, else 0.3 for similarity and 0.6 for coherence.

None penalty float

Residual weight factor per 2 pi cycle jump.

0.5 f0 float

Scale of the residual weight's decay with the distance to the nearest whole cycle.

0.25 min_residual float

Lowest residual weight: cycle jumps down-weight, never exclude.

0.05

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

weight (time, y, x) and static_weight (y, x), one weight_<layer> per layer, and for the residuals cycles, ambiguous and jump_fraction (share of dates with a jump). Lazy if the input is.

Examples:

>>> w = dxr.quality_weights(ds)
>>> fit = dxr.fit_trajectory(ds, weights=w.weight)

docs.title: weights
docs.text:
Quality weights from the DISP quality layers (PRD S2, plan task T26).

Each layer maps to a weight between 0 and 1, and the weights combine as a weighted geometric mean, prod(w_i ** (a_i / sum(a))):

phase_similarity, temporal_coherence (good near 1) Linear stretch clip((v - floor) / (1 - floor), 0, 1): values at or below the floor get weight 0 and exclude the pixel at that epoch. timeseries_inversion_residuals (good near 0) The per-date sum of absolute residuals, in radians, of dolphin's L1 time-series inversion over every interferogram that includes the date. An unwrapping error of one cycle in one interferogram adds about 2 pi to both of its dates, so on real granules the residuals cluster near multiples of 2 pi (residual_cycle_histogram). The residual splits into cycles = round(r / 2 pi) and the distance to that lattice frac = |r / 2 pi - cycles| (0 to 0.5). The weight is penalty ** cycles * exp(-frac / f0), clamped to min_residual so a cycle jump down-weights a pixel but never removes it (PRD decision). A frac near 0.5 is ambiguous between two cycle counts and is flagged.

The per-epoch weight (time, y, x) combines the per-epoch layer weights; the static weight (y, x) combines their time means, with the residual term replaced by one minus the share of dates that have a cycle jump.

Defaults for the floors, penalty, f0 and min_residual are provisional until the trade study (plan task T29).

docs.title: residual_cycles
docs.text:
residual_cycles(residuals: DataArray) -> xr.Dataset

Split inversion residuals into 2 pi cycles and the distance to them.

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

cycles (integer count of 2 pi), frac (0 to 0.5, distance to the nearest whole cycle) and ambiguous (frac within AMBIGUOUS_WIDTH of 0.5: the cycle count could be either).

Examples:

>>> r = xr.DataArray([0.1, 2 * np.pi + 0.2, 3 * np.pi], dims="time")
>>> residual_cycles(r).cycles.values.tolist()
[0, 1, 2]

docs.title: network_degree
docs.text:
network_degree(ds: Dataset, max_bandwidth: int) -> xr.DataArray

Return the interferogram count of each epoch's date in its ministack.

In a bandwidth-limited network each date pairs with up to max_bandwidth neighbours on each side within its ministack, whose first date is the (compressed) reference. A secondary at position p of N dates has min(p, b) + min(N - 1 - p, b) interferograms.

Returns None if the config is missing or the network is not bandwidth-limited.

docs.title: residual_cycle_histogram
docs.text:
residual_cycle_histogram(ds: Dataset, bins: Optional[ndarray] = None, min_residual: float = 0.05) -> pd.Series

Histogram of the inversion residuals in units of 2 pi.

On real DISP-S1 granules the counts peak near whole numbers (one 2 pi unwrapping error per interferogram), which the cycle decomposition of :func:quality_weights assumes. Residuals below min_residual radians (clean pixels) are left out so the peaks show.

docs.title: NaNPolicy

How a NaN at a crossover epoch affects later ministacks.

docs.text:
predict_trajectory(fit: Dataset, times: Union[ndarray, Sequence], dtype: str = 'float32') -> xr.DataArray

Evaluate a fitted trajectory at times (lazily if the fit is).

The model is rebuilt from the coefficient names and the reference time in fit.attrs, so a fit read back from a store can be evaluated. Computed in dtype and never stored unless you write it.

docs.title: Velocity for every pixel
docs.text:
Velocity for every pixel: OLS, Whittle colored noise, or MIDAS.

fit_velocity(ds, method=...) runs per pixel on a full frame:

"ols" The linear term of :func:~disp_xr.timeseries.trajectory.fit_trajectory, with white-noise sigmas (too small for real InSAR series). "whittle" The same OLS velocity, with noise estimated per pixel from the periodogram of the OLS residuals (Whittle likelihood, power law plus white): kappa, the white fraction and amplitudes, and the colored-noise sigma of the velocity. Reliable from about 200 epochs; on short records it underestimates |kappa| and the sigma (benchmarks/whittle_bias.py). The sigma uses the covariance of the complete record, so it is approximate for pixels with gaps, and the amplitudes come from the gap-filled grid, which interpolation smooths (about 10% low with 20% gaps). The exact grouped GLS is plan task T23. "midas" The median of slopes between epoch pairs about one year apart, trimmed at two scaled MADs (Blewitt et al., 2016): robust to outliers, seasonal signals and steps, with its own sigma. A step biases it when the pairs that span it are a large share, about one year over the record length, so prefer records of several years. Pairs are chosen from the stack dates; a pair with a NaN end is dropped, where per-series MIDAS would choose a replacement.

Blewitt, G., Kreemer, C., Hammond, W. C., & Gazeaux, J. (2016). MIDAS robust trend estimator for accurate GPS station velocities without step detection. JGR Solid Earth, 121, 2054-2068. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015JB012552

docs.title: fit_velocity
docs.text:
fit_velocity(obj: Union[Dataset, DataArray], method: Literal['ols', 'whittle', 'midas', 'gls'] = 'whittle', *, terms: Optional[Trajectory] = None, layer: str = 'displacement', min_valid: int = 0, noise: str = 'PLWN', groups: Union[str, DataArray] = 'coherence', n_groups: int = 5, n_samples: int = 16, allow_denoised: bool = False) -> xr.Dataset

Estimate a velocity and its sigma for every pixel.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default obj Dataset or DataArray

Chained displacement (time, y, x), or a Dataset holding it.

required method ('whittle', 'gls', 'ols', 'midas')

"whittle" (default): colored-noise sigmas, reliable from about 200 epochs (6.5 years at 12 days); a warning is logged below. "gls": exact generalized least squares, with the noise shape estimated per group of pixels by exact maximum likelihood and the amplitude per pixel; works on short records too, costs more. "midas": robust to unmodelled steps and outliers, for records of several years. "ols": fast, but its sigma ignores correlated noise and is several times too small. For shorter records use :func:disp_xr.fit_noise on selected pixels. See the guide "Choosing a velocity method" in the documentation.

"whittle" terms Trajectory

Deterministic model for "ols" and "whittle" (default offset, velocity and annual cycle). MIDAS needs none.

None layer str

Layer of a Dataset.

'displacement' min_valid int

Fewest valid epochs to fit a pixel ("ols", "whittle", "gls").

0 noise ('PLWN', 'FNWN', 'RWFNWN', 'WN', 'auto')

Noise model of "gls"; "auto" picks FNWN, PLWN or RWFNWN per group by the median BIC of its sampled pixels.

"PLWN" groups 'coherence' or DataArray

"gls" groups: n_groups quantile bins of time-mean temporal_coherence (needs the Dataset), or an integer label map (y, x); -1 leaves a pixel out.

'coherence' n_groups int

Coherence bins, and pixels per group fitted to estimate its noise.

5 n_samples int

Coherence bins, and pixels per group fitted to estimate its noise.

5 allow_denoised bool

Fit data marked attrs["denoised"]. Off by default: velocities and their sigmas come from the raw series (PRD S1).

False

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

velocity and velocity_sigma (unit per year) for every method; kappa, sigma_powerlaw, sigma_white and n_valid for Whittle; outlier_fraction and velocity_scatter for MIDAS; noise_amplitude, noise_group, kappa, white_fraction and n_valid for GLS, with the group table in attrs["noise_groups"] (JSON). Lazy if the input is, except the sampled pixels GLS reads to estimate the noise.

Examples:

>>> vel = dxr.fit_velocity(ds, "midas")

docs.title: gls
docs.text:
Full-frame velocity by generalized least squares with colored noise (T23).

The noise covariance of a pixel depends on the epochs, which of them are valid, and the noise parameters, not on the pixel's values. So the covariance shape (the spectral index and the mix of noise components) is estimated per group of pixels, by exact maximum likelihood (:func:~disp_xr.timeseries.noise.fit_noise) on a sample of each group's pixels, and every pixel is then fitted by exact GLS under its group's shape, with its own noise amplitude profiled from its residuals. Each pixel gets a colored-noise velocity sigma without an n x n factorization per pixel.

Groups are quantile bins of time-averaged temporal_coherence by default, or any integer label map (for example quadtree cells, plan task T28).

Missing epochs. Each group's covariance over the complete record is inverted once, Q = C⁻¹. For a pixel missing the epochs m, the inverse covariance of its valid epochs is the Schur complement P = Q - Q[:, m] Q[m, m]⁻¹ Q[m, :], which is zero on the missing rows and columns. The normal equations and residual quadratic forms follow from Q, Q A and a k x k inverse per pixel (k = len(m)), batched over pixels with the same k.

docs.title: NoiseShape dataclass
docs.text:
Covariance shape of a group: components (kappa, weight), weights sum to 1.

The covariance of a pixel is sigma2 * sum(w * C(kappa)) over the components, with C(0) the identity and sigma2 the pixel's own amplitude.

docs.text:
kappa: float

Spectral index of the power-law component (NaN for mixtures).

docs.title: white_fraction property
docs.text:
white_fraction: float

Share of the variance in the white component.

docs.text:
covariance(obs_idx: ndarray) -> np.ndarray

Return the unit-amplitude covariance at the grid indices obs_idx.

Label pixels by quantile bin of their (time-mean) temporal_coherence.

docs.title: estimate_group_noise
docs.text:
estimate_group_noise(da: DataArray, labels: DataArray, *, terms: Trajectory, noise: str = 'PLWN', n_samples: int = 16, seed: int = 0, max_workers: Optional[int] = None) -> dict[int, NoiseShape]

Estimate a noise shape per group from a random sample of its pixels.

Each sampled pixel is fitted with :func:fit_noise (exact RMLE); the group shape is the median of the samples' shapes. With noise="auto", FNWN, PLWN and RWFNWN are fitted and the model with the lowest median BIC is used for the group.

docs.title: Model diagnostics
docs.text:
Per-pixel diagnostics of a fitted trajectory model (PRD S4, plan T32.6b-c).

:func:model_diagnostics describes the residuals of every pixel's fit: mean, standard deviation, skewness, excess kurtosis, autocorrelation at chosen lags and the Anderson-Darling statistic for normality. White-noise sigmas (the sigma of :func:disp_xr.fit_trajectory) hold only when the residuals are uncorrelated and Gaussian; autocorrelation above about 0.3 or an Anderson-Darling statistic above about 0.75 (the 5% critical value) says they are optimistic, and :func:disp_xr.fit_velocity with a colored-noise method is the better tool. The model is evaluated on the fly from the coefficients (:func:disp_xr.predict_trajectory), never stored, and every statistic comes from one pass per block of pixels over time-contiguous chunks.

:func:significance turns coefficients and sigmas into z-scores, two-sided p-values and confidence intervals.

The statistics follow the Brisbane notebook (branch _stats_analysis.py), with Anderson-Darling vectorized over pixels in NumPy instead of a per-pixel apply_ufunc(vectorize=True).

docs.text:
model_diagnostics(data: Union[Dataset, DataArray], fit: Dataset, *, layer: str = 'displacement', lags: Sequence[int] = (1,)) -> xr.Dataset

Describe the residuals of a trajectory fit at every pixel, lazily.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Dataset or DataArray

The data that were fitted, (time, y, x).

required fit Dataset

:func:disp_xr.fit_trajectory output for data.

required layer str

Layer of a Dataset.

'displacement' lags sequence of int

Lags, in epochs, of the residual autocorrelation.

(1,)

(y, x): n (residuals used), residual_mean, residual_std, skewness, kurtosis (excess), autocorrelation_lag<k> and anderson_darling (normality; above AD_CRITICAL_5 rejects at 5%).

Examples:

>>> fit = dxr.fit_trajectory(ds)
>>> diag = model_diagnostics(ds, fit, lags=(1, 2))
>>> (diag.autocorrelation_lag1 > 0.3).mean()

docs.title: anderson_darling
docs.text:
anderson_darling(values: ndarray, axis: int = -1) -> np.ndarray

Return the Anderson-Darling normality statistic along axis, ignoring NaN.

Mean and variance are estimated from the data, with Stephens' small-sample correction A² (1 + 0.75 / n + 2.25 / n²). Vectorized: one sort for all series. NaN where fewer than 8 values are finite.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

True

docs.title: Time grids, gaps and breaks
docs.text:
Regular time grids, refused gaps and declared breaks (PRD S3, plan task T30).

Rules from the temporal-denoising study (Kiritimati DISP-S1, 2026-09):

  • Grid step. 15 d where sampling is genuinely 12-day, 30 d for 24-day sampling. A 15-day grid is finer than 24-day sampling supports. The step is chosen from the 75th percentile of the acquisition intervals rather than the median: the study's pre segment has a 12-day median (18 of its 34 intervals) but 14 intervals of 24 days, and the study recommends 30 d for such frames. The step is 15 d per 12 d of that percentile, rounded.
  • Gaps are refused, not interpolated. A grid point farther than max_gap_days / 2 from every acquisition lies inside a hole longer than max_gap_days and is marked; a 15-day grid across pre's 288-day hole would otherwise invent about 19 samples.
  • Breaks are declared (earthquake catalogs, user input); no automatic detection before 1.0. A break at tb lands on the first epoch at or after it: the first observation that already contains the jump. Filters that know nothing about discontinuities respect them when run per segment (:func:apply_segmented).

docs.title: regular_time_grid
docs.text:
regular_time_grid(times: TimesLike, step: Optional[int] = None, *, start: Optional[Any] = None, end: Optional[Any] = None) -> pd.DatetimeIndex

grid_step_days(times: TimesLike) -> int

Return the grid step in days for these acquisitions (15 per 12 d of sampling).

Uses the 75th percentile of the intervals, so a frame with a mix of 12- and 24-day intervals gets 30 d (see the module docstring).

docs.text:
gap_mask(times: TimesLike, grid: TimesLike, max_gap_days: Optional[float] = None) -> np.ndarray

Return True for grid dates inside a refused gap.

A grid date farther than max_gap_days / 2 from every acquisition lies in a hole longer than max_gap_days; resampled values there must be NaN, never interpolated.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default times array of datetimes

Acquisition times.

required grid array of datetimes

Grid dates (for example :func:regular_time_grid).

required max_gap_days float

Longest hole to bridge; default four times the typical (75th percentile) interval, so a missed acquisition or two is bridged and a season-long hole is not.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Boolean, one per grid date.

Examples:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> times = pd.to_datetime(["2020-01-01", "2020-01-13", "2020-09-01"])
>>> grid = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", "2020-09-01", freq="30D")
>>> gap_mask(times, grid, max_gap_days=60).sum()

apply_segmented(fn: Callable, data: Union[DataArray, Dataset, ndarray], breaks: Optional[Sequence[Any]], *, times: Optional[TimesLike] = None, min_len: int = 3) -> Any

Run fn on each segment between breaks independently.

A filter that knows nothing about discontinuities then never smooths across one, at the cost of one-sided support at each segment edge.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default fn callable

For xarray input, fn(segment) -> segment on the time slice (same shape). For NumPy input, fn(t_segment, y_segment) with y of shape (time, ...).

required data (DataArray, Dataset or ndarray)

Series with time first (NumPy) or a time dimension (xarray).

required breaks sequence of date-like

Break dates.

required times array of datetimes

Acquisition times for NumPy input (xarray uses its time).

None min_len int

Segments shorter than this are passed through unchanged: one or two epochs carry nothing a smoother could use.

3

Returns:

Type Description Same type as ``data``.

Examples:

>>> breaks = ["2023-02-06"]
>>> smooth = apply_segmented(my_filter, ds.displacement, breaks)

docs.title: Temporal denoising
docs.text:
Temporal denoising: gated Kalman smoother and robust LOWESS (PRD S3, T31).

Both methods share one interface, :func:denoise, and evaluate on the acquisitions or on a regular grid (:func:disp_xr.timeseries.regular_time_grid) with refused gaps. They are for display, resampling, linearity checks and transient hunting: the temporal-denoising study (Kiritimati DISP-S1, 2026-09) found that no filter improves a velocity, because InSAR residuals at 12-day sampling are white and ordinary least squares is already optimal. Fit rates on the raw series; :func:disp_xr.fit_trajectory refuses data marked as denoised.

Kalman (method="kalman"): a local-linear-trend model (displacement and velocity, an integrated random walk) with a Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother, or a fixed-lag smoother for products that publish as data arrive. The only knobs are the timescale tau_days (20 to 30 d), which sets the process noise q = 3 R / tau³ against the measurement variance R (estimated per pixel from the data), and the χ² gate: an update whose normalized innovation squared exceeds gate (9) is skipped. A one-epoch outlier makes one huge innovation and is rejected; a real transient builds over several epochs that stay inside the gate. In the study it left 0.2 to 0.4% of an injected spike and kept 93% of a 60-day transient. Declared breaks inflate the covariance at the first epoch after them (break_mode: offset, rate or both), and the gate is suspended there, so a real step is kept; the inflated covariance also stops the backward pass at the break.

Unlike the study, each pixel keeps its own 2 x 2 covariance: DISP pixels have their own missing epochs, and the study's production notes ask for a per-pixel gate (unwrapping jumps) rather than its scene-wide one.

LOWESS (method="lowess"): robust local-linear regression (tricube kernel of bandwidth_days, 60 d, and iterations bisquare reweightings, 2, per pixel), defined at any time. Its outlier rejection depends on sampling density (0.1% of a spike survives at 12-day sampling, about 30% at 24-day). Breaks are handled by fitting each segment separately.

Known limitation: both methods were evaluated on one flat, aseismic site (Kiritimati). A deforming site with topography-correlated troposphere is part of the T29 trade-study frames.

docs.title: q_from_timescale
docs.text:
q_from_timescale(tau_days: float, r: Union[float, ndarray]) -> Any

Return the process noise giving a smoothing timescale of tau_days.

For an integrated random walk the timescale where process noise balances measurement noise r is tau = (3 r / q)^(1/3) (in years). Setting q directly is how a filter silently returns a straight line (q too small for r).

docs.title: lowess
docs.text:
lowess(t_years: ndarray, y: ndarray, t_out: ndarray, *, bandwidth_days: float = 60.0, iterations: int = 2, min_points: int = 3) -> np.ndarray

Robust local-linear regression of (time, npix) series at t_out.

The window at each output time is bandwidth_days wide on each side, widened to the min_points nearest acquisitions where sampling is sparse; pixels with fewer than min_points valid values in it are NaN. Each of iterations passes reweights points by the bisquare of their residual over six times the pixel's median absolute residual (Cleveland 1979, https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1979.10481038).

docs.title: Colored noise (one series)
docs.text:
Colored-noise trend estimation for one time series (maximum likelihood).

The deterministic model (a :class:~disp_xr.timeseries.trajectory.Trajectory or any design matrix) is fitted by generalized least squares inside the likelihood of a noise model, and the noise parameters are estimated by (restricted) maximum likelihood. The resulting sigmas account for temporal correlation, which ordinary least squares ignores: for GNSS and InSAR series OLS velocity sigmas are often 5 to 10 times too small.

Noise models:

"WN" White noise only (equivalent to OLS). "FNWN" Flicker (spectral index -1) plus white. "PLWN" Power law with a free spectral index kappa plus white. "RWFNWN" Random walk (-2), flicker and white.

Each likelihood evaluation factorizes an n x n covariance (O(n³)), so this is for one series or a group of pixels; full frames use the vectorized estimators of plan task T22. method="whittle" estimates the noise from the periodogram of the OLS residuals (O(n log n)) and makes one exact GLS solve.

The method follows Hector / HectorP (Bos et al.), written from the papers:

  • Bos, M. S., Fernandes, R. M. S., Williams, S. D. P., & Bastos, L. (2013). Fast error analysis of continuous GNSS observations with missing data. Journal of Geodesy, 87(4), 351-360. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00190-012-0605-0
  • Williams, S. D. P. (2003). The effect of coloured noise on the uncertainties of rates estimated from geodetic time series. Journal of Geodesy, 76(9-10), 483-494. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00190-002-0283-4
  • Hosking, J. R. M. (1981). Fractional differencing. Biometrika, 68(1), 165-176. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/68.1.165

Fit a trajectory to one series under a colored-noise model.

Epochs; need not be regular. NaN values in y are dropped.

The series (any unit; outputs use the same unit).

required design ndarray

(time, coefficient) design matrix. By default built from terms.

None terms Trajectory

Model terms when design is not given; default offset, velocity and an annual cycle.

None names sequence of str

Coefficient names for a given design.

None model ('PLWN', 'FNWN', 'RWFNWN', 'WN')

Noise model; see the module docstring.

"PLWN" rmle bool

Restricted maximum likelihood, which corrects the noise estimate for the degrees of freedom used by the deterministic model.

True method ('exact', 'whittle')

Time-domain (R)MLE (O(n³) per evaluation), or the noise from the Whittle likelihood of the OLS residuals (O(n log n)) followed by one exact GLS solve. Whittle supports PLWN and WN.

docs.title: Downsampling
docs.text:
Quality-weighted downsampling to hexagonal cells (PRD S2 hexagon mode, T27.8).

Pixels are grouped into pointy-top hexagons of a planar lattice in the frame's CRS, anchored at the CRS origin, so overlapping frames of one UTM zone share cell ids. spacing is the distance between neighboring cell centers (the flat-to-flat width); a hexagon covers sqrt(3) / 2 * spacing², so spacing = 1.0746 * side matches the area of a square of that side.

Each pixel goes to the hexagon whose center is nearest, found with axial coordinates and cube rounding (Patel, "Hexagonal Grids", Red Blob Games). The per-cell statistics are those of :func:disp_xr.downsample (weighted mean or median, sigma, n_eff, valid fraction, quality, weighted centroid, mode or "any" for masks and labels), computed with grouped sums (one np.bincount per dask block) instead of block sums. Hexagons are not a raster, so the result is a (time, point) table in the :func:disp_xr.to_points layout.

Why hexagons: all six neighbors are equidistant and a hexagon is more compact than a square of equal area, so the sampling is more isotropic (Birch et al. 2007, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2007.03.041). The lattice is the one matplotlib.hexbin and PostGIS ST_HexagonGrid build (Carr et al. 1987, https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478445); here the cells carry quality weights and sigmas, lazily.

docs.title: downsample
docs.text:
Quality-weighted downsampling to a regular coarse grid (PRD S2, plan task T27).

Each output cell aggregates a factor x factor block of 30 m pixels:

  • float layers: the weighted mean (stat="wmean") or weighted median (stat="wmedian"), with the weighted spread, the effective sample count n_eff = (Σw)² / Σw² and sigma = spread / sqrt(n_eff);
  • integer mask and label layers: the most common value ("mode") or whether any pixel is set ("any"), never a mean.

With spread, each float layer also gets its spatial variation within the cell, all weighted with the same weights: <layer>_std (weighted standard deviation of the pixels), <layer>_rmse (weighted RMS of the pixels about the cell value; equal to the std for "wmean") and <layer>_mad (weighted median of the absolute deviations from the weighted median; times 1.4826 it estimates the std of Gaussian data).

Every cell also gets n_valid, valid_fraction (of the full block, so edge cells padded beyond the frame show how much they hold) and quality (mean static weight). Weighted-mean levels keep sum_w and sum_w2 so a coarser mean can be rebuilt from them; a weighted median cannot, so every median level is computed from 30 m. The sigma treats pixels as independent, which is far too small at 1 to 10 km; pass a variogram model (:mod:disp_xr.residuals) to also get <layer>_sigma_corr, which accounts for spatially correlated errors.

Odd factors (33, 67, 333 for 990 m, 2,010 m, 9,990 m) put each cell centre on a 30 m pixel centre, so the coarse transform is exact. Run after chaining and re-referencing: averaging series with different reference dates is wrong.

docs.title: downsample
docs.text:
downsample(ds: Dataset, *, factor: Optional[int] = None, spacing: Optional[float] = None, stat: Stat = 'wmean', weights: Union[str, DataArray, None] = 'quality', layers: Optional[list[str]] = None, categorical: Optional[Mapping[str, Categorical]] = None, nan_threshold: float = 1.0, variogram: Optional[Mapping[str, VariogramModel]] = None, spread: Union[Spread, Sequence[Spread], None] = None) -> xr.Dataset

Aggregate a DISP dataset to coarse cells with quality weights.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ds Dataset

Chained, re-referenced data with y and x (and optionally time) dimensions.

required factor int

Pixels per cell side. Odd factors keep cell centres on pixel centres (33, 67, 333 for about 1, 2 and 10 km at 30 m).

None spacing float

Cell size in the CRS unit instead of factor; rounded to the nearest odd factor.

None stat ('wmean', 'wmedian')

Weighted mean or weighted median of float layers.

"wmean" weights ('quality', DataArray or None)

"quality" (default): :func:disp_xr.quality_weights from the quality layers present, per epoch when the data have time. A DataArray (time, y, x) or (y, x) of weights, or None for equal weights.

'quality' layers list of str

Float layers to aggregate; default every float layer with y and x except quality layers used for the weights.

None categorical mapping

Mask and label layers and their reduction, "mode" or "any"; defaults in CATEGORICAL_DEFAULTS (mode for masks and labels, any for persistent scatterers and layover/shadow). Other integer layers (counts) are averaged like floats, ignoring their fill value.

None nan_threshold float

Largest share of missing pixels (of the full block) a cell may have; cells above it become NaN. 1.0 keeps any cell with data. Follows xarray-regrid's nan_threshold.

1.0 variogram mapping of str to VariogramModel

A fitted variogram (:func:disp_xr.residuals.fit_variogram) per layer, estimated on that layer's residual field. Adds <layer>_sigma_corr = sqrt(sill / n_eff_corr) and n_eff_corr, the effective number of independent pixels of the cell mean given the spatial correlation (Hugonnet et al. 2022). The model is the same for every epoch.

None spread ('std', 'rmse', 'mad')

Spatial variation of each float layer within the cell, weighted with the same weights: <layer>_std (weighted standard deviation), <layer>_rmse (weighted RMS about the cell value; equals the std for "wmean", and adds the mean-median offset for "wmedian") and <layer>_mad (weighted median absolute deviation from the weighted median; robust to outlier pixels). Per epoch when the data have time. Unlike <layer>_sigma, these describe the pixels, not the uncertainty of the cell value.

"std"

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

One variable per aggregated layer on the coarse grid, with <layer>_sigma and, shared by all, n_eff, n_valid, valid_fraction, quality, centroid_x, centroid_y, and for "wmean" sum_w and sum_w2; with variogram, <layer>_sigma_corr and n_eff_corr; with spread, <layer>_std, <layer>_rmse or <layer>_mad. Integer layers are reduced with mode or any. Lazy if the input is.

Examples:

>>> coarse = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=33)
>>> points = dxr.to_points(coarse)
>>> robust = dxr.downsample(
...     ds, factor=67, stat="wmedian", spread="mad"
... )
>>> robust.displacement_mad

docs.text:
to_points(coarse: Dataset, min_valid_fraction: float = 0.0) -> xr.Dataset

Return the occupied cells of a downsampled dataset as points.

The result has dimension point (and time if present), ordered by cell row then column, with the weighted centroid (centroid_x, centroid_y), the cell centre (x, y), the cell id (row * n_cols + col) and every cell variable. .to_dataframe() gives the table.

Examples:

>>> coarse = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=33)
>>> points = dxr.to_points(coarse, min_valid_fraction=0.5)
>>> points.to_dataframe()

docs.title: quadtree
docs.text:
Quality-weighted quadtree downsampling (PRD S2 quadtree mode, plan task T28).

Cells of level k cover 2**k x 2**k pixels of the 30 m grid, anchored at its first pixel, from min_level (finest) to max_level (coarsest). A cell splits into its four children while its split score exceeds a threshold and every child keeps enough reliable pixels; the cells that do not split are the leaves. Smooth areas end up in large cells and areas with structure (deformation, unwrapping errors) in small ones.

The per-cell sums of :func:disp_xr.downsample (Σw, Σw², Σwv, Σwv², valid count) compose exactly: a level is the 2 x 2 block sum of the level below. So the data are read twice: once for the sums of the finest level (and from them every coarser level and every score), once for the values of the leaves. Leaf selection works on the small score maps, level by level, as boolean masks, with no recursion per cell.

Split metrics (metric):

  • "displacement": RMS over epochs of the weighted spread of the pixels in the cell, in the unit of the data, so a threshold reads as "split where pixels in a cell differ by more than 5 mm";
  • "velocity": weighted spread of a per-pixel velocity (pass velocity, for example from :func:disp_xr.fit_velocity), in its unit;
  • "structure": the spread of the four children's means divided by their noise (the mean of their sigmas), both RMS over epochs: signal structure at the cell scale against noise, after the structure function of GPS Imaging (Hammond et al. 2016, https://doi.org/10.1002/2016JB013458). Unitless; split above about 2;
  • or a callable metric(level, children) -> (y, x) DataArray that gets the level's sums as a Dataset and those of its children (None at min_level).

Plan task T29 compares the three and sets defaults.

docs.title: Correlated-error sigma
docs.text:
Residuals: spatial variograms (T27.3b) and DISP against GNSS (T32).

:func:compare compares DISP with GNSS at the stations, with geepers computing the metrics (see its docstring). The rest of this docstring covers the variograms.

The sigma of a cell mean computed as spread / sqrt(n) assumes independent pixels. InSAR errors (troposphere, unwrapping, orbits) are correlated over kilometres, so at 1 to 10 km cells that sigma is far too small. Following xDEM (Hugonnet et al. 2022), this module

  1. estimates an empirical variogram of a residual field (a field that should be zero: stable ground, or data minus a model) from a random sample of pixel pairs, with distances drawn log-uniformly so short lags are as well sampled as long ones (:func:empirical_variogram);
  2. fits a sum of spherical, exponential or Gaussian models and a nugget (:func:fit_variogram);
  3. turns the model into the effective number of independent samples of a block mean (:func:mean_block_correlation, :func:n_eff_correlated), which :func:disp_xr.downsample uses for <layer>_sigma_corr.

The residual semivariogram of plan task T32.1 reuses this code.

References

Hugonnet, R., et al. (2022). Uncertainty analysis of digital elevation models by spatial inference from stable terrain. IEEE JSTARS 15, 6456-6472. https://doi.org/10.1109/JSTARS.2022.3188922

Rolstad, C., Haug, T. and Denby, B. (2009). Spatially integrated geodetic glacier mass balance and its uncertainty based on geostatistical analysis. Journal of Glaciology 55(192), 666-680. https://doi.org/10.3189/002214309789470950

docs.title: empirical_variogram
docs.text:
empirical_variogram(field: DataArray, *, n_pairs: int = 200000, n_bins: int = 30, max_distance: Optional[float] = None, seed: int = 0) -> xr.Dataset

Estimate the empirical semivariogram of a 2D field from random pairs.

Each pair starts at a random valid pixel; its partner lies at a distance drawn log-uniformly between one pixel and max_distance, in a random direction. Every logarithmic distance bin then gets about the same number of pairs, unlike all pairs of a random sample, which leave short lags (where the cell sigma is decided) nearly empty.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default field DataArray

A (y, x) residual field, ideally zero-mean with no deformation signal (stable ground, or data minus a fitted model). NaN pixels are skipped. It is loaded into memory.

required n_pairs int

Number of pairs drawn (pairs whose partner is NaN or off the grid are dropped).

200000 n_bins int

Number of logarithmic distance bins.

30 max_distance float

Largest distance, in the CRS unit; default half the shorter side of the field.

None seed int

Random seed.

0

Returns:

Type Description Dataset

Dimension lag, with distance (mean pair distance in the bin, a coordinate), gamma (semivariance, half the mean squared difference) and count (pairs per bin). Empty bins are dropped.

Examples:

>>> residual = ds.displacement.isel(time=-1) - trend
>>> empirical = dxr.empirical_variogram(
...     residual, max_distance=20e3
... )

docs.title: fit_variogram
docs.text:
fit_variogram(empirical: Dataset, models: Sequence[ModelKind] = ('spherical', 'spherical'), *, nugget: bool = True) -> VariogramModel

Fit a nugget and a sum of models to an empirical variogram.

Weighted least squares with the approximate standard error of each bin, gamma * sqrt(2 / count), so every bin counts by its relative misfit and short lags are not swamped by the large semivariances of long ones. Two spherical models (a short and a long range) are xDEM's default for elevation residuals and fit InSAR residuals (turbulent troposphere plus long-wavelength errors) well.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default empirical Dataset

Output of :func:empirical_variogram.

required models sequence of {"spherical", "exponential", "gaussian"}

One entry per component, from short to long range.

('spherical', 'spherical') nugget bool

Fit a nugget (uncorrelated pixel noise); otherwise it is 0.

True

Returns:

Type Description VariogramModel

Examples:

>>> model = dxr.fit_variogram(empirical, ("exponential",))
>>> coarse = dxr.downsample(
...     ds, factor=33, variogram={"displacement": model}
... )

docs.title: VariogramModel dataclass
docs.text:
A nugget plus a sum of bounded variogram models.

gamma(h) = nugget + sum(sill_k * f_k(h / range_k)) for h > 0 and 0 at h = 0. Ranges are practical ranges (the semivariance reaches 95% of the partial sill for exponential and Gaussian models, all of it for spherical ones), in the CRS unit of the field.

Examples:

>>> model = dxr.fit_variogram(empirical)
>>> model.sill, model.ranges

docs.title: mean_block_correlation
docs.text:
mean_block_correlation(model: VariogramModel, factor: int, spacing: Union[float, tuple[float, float]]) -> float

Return the mean correlation between two distinct pixels of a block.

Exact for a full factor x factor block: the double sum over pixel pairs is a sum over the (2 factor - 1)² pixel offsets, each counted (factor - |dy|) (factor - |dx|) times.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default model VariogramModel

The fitted variogram.

required factor int

Pixels per block side.

required spacing float or (float, float)

Pixel spacing, or (dy, dx), in the unit of the model ranges.

required

Examples:

>>> rho = mean_block_correlation(model, factor=33, spacing=30.0)

docs.title: mean_mask_correlation
docs.text:
mean_mask_correlation(model: VariogramModel, mask: ndarray, spacing: Union[float, tuple[float, float]]) -> float

Return the mean correlation between two distinct pixels of a cell shape.

mask marks the pixels of one full cell (a hexagon, for example). The number of pixel pairs at each offset is the autocorrelation of the mask, computed with an FFT, so the double sum over pairs costs one transform. :func:mean_block_correlation is the square-block case.

Examples:

>>> rho = mean_mask_correlation(model, cell_mask, spacing=30.0)

docs.title: n_eff_correlated
docs.text:
n_eff_correlated(sum_w, sum_w2, rho_bar: float)

Return the effective sample count of a weighted mean of correlated pixels.

The variance of a weighted mean is sill * Σᵢⱼ wᵢ wⱼ ρᵢⱼ / (Σw)². Replacing each off-diagonal ρᵢⱼ by the block mean rho_bar gives n_eff = (Σw)² / (Σw² + ((Σw)² - Σw²) rho_bar): (Σw)² / Σw² for independent pixels, 1 for fully correlated ones. Exact for a full block with equal weights; it assumes valid pixels and weights are spread evenly over the block, so it overestimates n_eff (underestimates the sigma) for blocks whose valid pixels cluster, such as edge cells.

Examples:

>>> n_eff_correlated(sum_w=100.0, sum_w2=100.0, rho_bar=0.0)
100.0

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
Read-only REST service over disp-xr stores (PRD C7, plan task T40).

An xpublish <https://github.com/xpublish-community/xpublish>_ plugin that serves, under /datasets/{dataset_id}/disp/:

  • timeseries: the displacement series at a point (median over a buffer), with the quality layers the store holds and its reference date;
  • velocity: the stored velocity and its sigma at a point;
  • cells: a regular grid or a quadtree of a bounding box, as GeoJSON;
  • gnss: the station residuals and summary of :func:residuals.compare, written next to the cube by :meth:Comparison.to_zarr;
  • provenance: operation history, input granules and versions.

Nothing heavy runs on request (PRD C7): velocities and GNSS residuals are served only when the store holds them, and cells downsamples at most MAX_CELL_PIXELS pixels. xpublish adds its own routes (Zarr over HTTP, dataset info) and, when installed, xpublish-tiles adds web map tiles. Every response carries the CRS and the units.

Start a service with disp_xr serve STORE or :func:make_app.

docs.title: tutorial
docs.text:
Synthetic OPERA DISP granules with a known truth, for examples and tests.

make_disp_stack(directory) writes a small frame of granules that open like real ones, and returns the displacement they were built from, so a result can be checked against the truth. The gallery and the test suite use it.

The files copy the layout of real granules (see tests/data/disp_s1_layout.md): one 2D (y, x) layer per variable, chunked and gzip-compressed with shuffle, a length-1 time coordinate, a reference_time variable, a spatial_ref grid mapping, and the /corrections, /identification and /metadata groups. Each ministack's reference date is the last secondary date of the previous ministack, as in real frames.

Request a stack by variant name through :func:make_disp_stack.

make_gnss_source(ds, pixels, cache_dir) serves synthetic GNSS stations that follow the DISP displacement at given pixels, through the geepers source interface, so :func:disp_xr.gnss.load and :func:disp_xr.residuals.compare run without a network (gnss extra). vertical_los(ds) gives matching static layers.

required variant str

One of :data:VARIANTS:

  • two_ministacks: 2 ministacks, one reference change.
  • three_ministacks: 3 ministacks, two reference changes.
  • with_gaps: 2 ministacks with two secondaries of the first removed.
  • duplicate: two_ministacks plus an older-version copy of one granule (path in extra["duplicate"]).

docs.title: correlated_noise
docs.text:
correlated_noise(shape: tuple[int, int], *, correlation_range: float, sill: float = 1.0, nugget: float = 0.0, spacing: float = SPACING, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray

Return a Gaussian random field with a known exponential covariance.

The covariance is sill * exp(-3 h / correlation_range) (practical range correlation_range, the convention of :class:disp_xr.residuals.VariogramModel) plus nugget of white noise, so variogram and cell-sigma estimates can be checked against the truth. Exact, by circulant embedding on a grid twice the size.

docs.title: make_gnss_source
docs.text:
make_gnss_source(ds: Dataset, pixels: list[tuple[int, int]], cache_dir: str | Path, *, noise: float = 0.001, extra_rate: dict[int, float] | None = None, seed: int = 0)

Return a geepers GNSS source whose stations follow DISP at pixels.

Each station sits at a (row, col) pixel; its daily up motion is that pixel's displacement (interpolated to days) plus white noise, with east and north zero, so it matches DISP under a vertical line of sight (:func:vertical_los). Needs the gnss extra (geepers).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ds Dataset

Chained, re-referenced DISP with a CRS.

required pixels list of (int, int)

Station pixels; stations are named S000, S001...

required cache_dir str or Path

geepers cache directory (nothing is downloaded).

required noise float

Standard deviation of the daily noise and the station sigmas (m).

0.001 extra_rate dict

Station index to an added up rate (m/yr), to make an outlier.

None seed int

Seed of the noise.

0

docs.title: Chunks for maps and time series¶
docs.text: DISP stores one file per date. A pixel's time series must open every file; a map needs one. disp-xr opens data lazily in the layout of the files, one epoch and one block per dask chunk, and each operation reads only what it touches. This example counts what each question reads.

docs.title: A map of one chained epoch¶
docs.text: Chaining adds, to each epoch, the displacement accumulated at the crossover epochs of earlier ministacks. The last epoch of three ministacks therefore reads itself and two crossovers, not the whole stack.

docs.title: A pixel's time series¶
docs.text: A series reads one block from every granule: all epochs, but only the block that holds the pixel.

docs.title: Choosing a layout¶
docs.text: Functions that work along time per pixel (fits, statistics) rechunk to whole time series themselves. When one kind of access repeats, rechunk once:

docs.title: Velocity with colored-noise uncertainty¶
docs.text:
Least-squares sigmas assume every epoch is independent. InSAR noise is correlated in time, so those sigmas are too small. fit_velocity(method= "gls") estimates the noise shape per group of pixels by exact maximum likelihood and fits every pixel by generalized least squares, so each pixel gets a colored-noise sigma.

The frame here is synthetic: a velocity gradient, flicker noise plus white noise, three times noisier in the left half (where coherence is lower).

docs.title: Fit¶
docs.text: Two coherence groups; 16 pixels of each are fitted exactly to estimate the group's noise shape (spectral index and white fraction). Every pixel's amplitude is its own.

docs.title: Sigmas¶
docs.text: The OLS sigma is several times smaller everywhere; GLS also sees that the left half is noisier.

docs.title: Are the sigmas honest?¶
docs.text: The truth is known, so count how often the velocity error falls within two sigmas: about 95% for an honest sigma.

docs.title: The command line, end to end¶
docs.text:
disp_xr runs the common steps without Python:

Command What it does search find a frame's granules in NASA CMR info summarize local granules: frame, dates, versions, duplicates stack correct, mask, chain and re-reference into one store export write COG, GeoTIFF, Zarr, GeoZarr (for bowser), NetCDF or MintPy geometry download the static layers (LOS, DEM, masks) on the DISP grid virtual build a virtual frame in Icechunk without copying data

This page runs info, stack and export on synthetic granules. Finding and downloading real ones looks like this (it needs Earthdata credentials in ~/.netrc):

disp_xr search --frame-id 11116 --start 2024-01-01 --out granules.csv
disp_xr geometry F11116/ --out static/

docs.title: What is in a folder of granules¶
One stack¶
docs.text: stack applies the steps in the product's order: subtract the corrections the product has not applied, apply the recommended mask, chain the ministacks, then re-reference (auto by default). The output is a Zarr store, or NetCDF with .nc, laid out for time series (--preset timeseries) or maps (--preset maps).

docs.title: Export¶
docs.text: export reads a store from stack (or granules, chained without corrections, masking or re-referencing) and writes other formats. Here, a Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF of the last epoch, and a GeoZarr store that the bowser viewer opens directly (--flat: this frame is too small for the display pyramid that full frames get).

docs.title: Back in Python¶
docs.text: Every output records where it came from: input granules, the steps and their parameters, and package versions.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr

import disp_xr as dxr
from disp_xr.timeseries import gap_mask, regular_time_grid

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
days = np.concatenate(
    [np.arange(0, 408, 12), np.arange(420, 700, 24), np.arange(900, 1500, 12)]
)
times = pd.Timestamp("2018-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(days, "D")
years = days / 365.25
truth = (
    -0.012 * years  # subsidence, 12 mm/yr
    + 0.004 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * years)  # 4 mm annual cycle
    + 0.010 * (days >= 1100)  # 10 mm step
    + 0.008 * np.exp(-(((days - 1300) / 30.0) ** 2))  # 8 mm transient
)
noisy = truth + 0.002 * rng.standard_normal((4, days.size))
noisy[:, 50] += 0.028  # unwrapping error: half a wavelength on one date
series = xr.DataArray(
    noisy.T[:, :, None],
    dims=("time", "y", "x"),
    coords={"time": times, "y": np.arange(4.0), "x": [0.0]},
    attrs={"units": "meters"},
)
intervals = sorted({int(d) for d in np.diff(days)})
print(f"{days.size} acquisitions, intervals {intervals} days")

def rms_mm(a):
    """Return the RMS of ``a`` in millimeters."""
    return 1e3 * float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean(np.square(a))))


spike = 50
transient = np.abs(days - 1300) <= 30

        f"transient kept {kept:.0%}"
    )
step = times[days >= 1100][0] kalman = dxr.denoise(series, "kalman", tau_days=20, breaks=[step]).compute() lowess = dxr.denoise(series, "lowess", bandwidth_days=60, breaks=[step]).compute() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4), layout="constrained") ax.plot(times, 1e3 * series.isel(y=0, x=0), ".", color="0.6", label="data") ax.plot(times, 1e3 * truth, "k-", lw=1, label="truth") ax.plot(times, 1e3 * kalman.isel(y=0, x=0), label="kalman, tau 20 d") ax.plot(times, 1e3 * lowess.isel(y=0, x=0), label="lowess, 60 d") ax.set(ylabel="displacement (mm)") ax.legend(ncols=4, loc="lower left") plt.show() def rms_mm(a): """Return the RMS of ``a`` in millimeters.""" return 1e3 * float(np.sqrt(np.nanmean(np.square(a)))) spike = 50 transient = np.abs(days - 1300) <= 30 base = truth - 0.008 * np.exp(-(((days - 1300) / 30.0) ** 2)) for name, out in (("kalman", kalman), ("lowess", lowess)): pixel = out.isel(y=0, x=0).values kept = (pixel - base)[transient].mean() / (truth - base)[transient].mean() print( f"{name}: error {rms_mm(out.values[:, :, 0].T - truth):.1f} mm RMS, " f"spike left {1e3 * (pixel[spike] - truth[spike]):.1f} mm of 28, " f"transient kept {kept:.0%}" ) 
kalman: error 0.9 mm RMS, spike left 0.4 mm of 28, transient kept 83%
lowess: error 1.0 mm RMS, spike left 0.7 mm of 28, transient kept 72%

Both remove the spike: the Kalman gate rejects the date, and LOWESS down-weights it through its robust passes. Both keep the step, because it is declared. They differ on the transient, a signal of about two months: the Kalman filter keeps more of it than the 60-day LOWESS window. A shorter tau_days or bandwidth_days keeps faster signals at the cost of more noise.

docs.title: Denoising time series and regular time grids¶
docs.text:
dxr.denoise smooths displacement series in time, for display and for resampling onto a regular grid. It has two methods with the same interface:

  • "kalman": a local-linear-trend Kalman filter with a smoother. It follows changes in rate over about tau_days, and a chi-square gate rejects outliers such as unwrapping jumps on single dates;
  • "lowess": robust locally weighted regression over bandwidth_days.

Neither improves a velocity estimate. Fit velocities on the raw series: denoised data carry attrs["denoised"], and the fits refuse them.

The series below has a known signal and irregular sampling like real DISP-S1 frames: 12-day revisits, some 24-day ones, and a 200-day hole. It also has a one-date spike (an unwrapping error), a step on a known date, and a short transient.

docs.title: On the acquisitions¶
docs.text: The step is declared with breaks=. Automatic break detection is out of scope: steps come from catalogs, such as earthquakes or equipment changes.

docs.title: On a regular grid¶
docs.text: grid="auto" resamples onto a regular grid. Its step comes from the sampling: 15 days for 12-day revisits, 30 days when 24-day intervals are common. Grid dates inside holes longer than max_gap_days are refused (NaN), not interpolated.

docs.title: Denoised data are for display¶
docs.text: The output records the method, and the fits refuse it unless asked explicitly. Smoothing correlates the residuals, so velocity sigmas from a denoised series would be far too small.

docs.title: Checking a velocity fit¶
docs.text:
fit_trajectory and fit_velocity(method="ols") give white-noise sigmas. Those hold only when the residuals are uncorrelated and Gaussian. DISP residuals often are not: troposphere and unwrapping leave correlated noise, and an unmodelled step leaves a long run of residuals of one sign. disp_xr.diagnostics checks this for every pixel:

  • model_diagnostics: residual mean, spread, skewness, kurtosis, autocorrelation at chosen lags and the Anderson-Darling normality statistic, in one pass over the data;
  • significance: z-scores, p-values and confidence intervals of the coefficients.

The frame below has three strips with the same 10 mm/yr velocity:

  • left: white noise, where the OLS sigmas are right;
  • middle: a random walk added, a correlated noise;
  • right: a 15 mm step that the model does not include.

docs.title: Fit and diagnose¶
docs.text: The trajectory model has an offset, the velocity and an annual cycle. model_diagnostics evaluates the model from the coefficients and reads the data once.

docs.title: How optimistic?¶
docs.text: A colored-noise method estimates the noise from the residuals' spectrum. Compare its velocity sigma with the OLS one in each strip.

docs.title: Significance¶
docs.text: significance gives each coefficient's z-score, p-value and confidence interval from the fit's sigmas. With white-noise sigmas on correlated residuals, almost everything looks significant. Use the colored-noise sigmas (or MIDAS) before reading the p-values.

docs.title: Downsampling with quality weights¶
docs.text: downsample aggregates 30 m pixels into coarse cells (about 1, 2 or 10 km) with quality weights, after chaining and re-referencing. Each cell gets a weighted mean or median, a sigma, the effective sample count, the share of the block that holds data and a quality score. to_points turns the cells into a point table for fits and GNSS comparison.

docs.title: Aggregate¶
docs.text: Factor 9 turns 30 m into 270 m cells here (on a real frame use 33, 67 or 333). Odd factors keep each cell centre on a pixel centre. Weights default to quality_weights (similarity, coherence and inversion residuals), per epoch.

docs.title: Spatial variation within a cell¶
docs.text: sigma is the uncertainty of the cell value. How much the pixels differ inside the cell is a different question, answered with spread: the weighted standard deviation (std), the weighted RMS about the cell value (rmse), and the weighted median absolute deviation from the weighted median (mad), which outlier pixels (unwrapping errors, a building) barely move. All use the same weights as the cell value. With a weighted median and mad, every statistic of the cell is robust. For Gaussian noise the MAD is about 0.67 times the std, as in the maps below (1.4826 MAD estimates the std).

docs.title: Sigma with spatially correlated errors¶
docs.text: InSAR errors (troposphere, unwrapping) are correlated over kilometres, so averaging 81 pixels does not divide the noise by 9. Following xDEM (Hugonnet et al. 2022), estimate a variogram on a residual field (stable ground, or data minus a model), fit it, and pass it to downsample. Here the residual is synthetic: correlated noise with a 900 m range, 2 mm correlated and 1 mm white.

docs.title: Hexagonal cells¶
docs.text: downsample_hex groups pixels into hexagons instead of squares: all six neighbors are equidistant, so the sampling is more isotropic. The lattice is anchored at the CRS origin, so overlapping frames of one UTM zone share cells. A spacing of 1.0746 times a square's side gives the same area; here 290 m hexagons next to the 270 m squares. The statistics are the same, and the result is a point table like to_points.

docs.title: Quadtree¶
docs.text:
quadtree keeps large cells where the data are smooth and splits them where they vary. Levels are factor-2 cells from 2^min_level pixels; a cell splits while its score is above the threshold and its four children keep enough reliable pixels. With metric="displacement" the score is the RMS weighted spread of the pixels in the cell, in meters. to_raster paints the leaves back on the 30 m grid.

Which to use: in the T29 trade study (three DISP-S1 frames, report), the regular grid of downsample reconstructed the 30 m field better than any quadtree with the same number of points, and agreed better with GNSS except across a creeping fault. Use the grid by default and the quadtree for sharp, local gradients. The quadtree's default metric is "structure", which splits where the four children differ by more than their noise; the displacement metric used here reads in meters and, on real frames, splits noisy cells first. For Cal/Val accuracy runs, a stricter coherence floor in the weights (dxr.quality_weights(ds, floors={"temporal_coherence": 0.8})) agreed better with GNSS, at the cost of 12 to 39% of the pixels.

docs.title: Exporting results¶
docs.text: disp-xr writes Zarr v3, NetCDF, Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) and MintPy inputs. Every output records the disp-xr version, the input granules and the operations applied, so a file can be traced back to its sources.

docs.title: Zarr¶
docs.text: The "timeseries" preset puts the whole time axis in each chunk, for per-pixel work; "maps" puts one epoch in each chunk, for viewing. Both use sharding and zstd compression.

docs.title: NetCDF and Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF¶
docs.text: to_geotiff writes a COG: tiled, with internal overviews once the image is larger than 512 pixels. Pass the Dataset and a layer so the file keeps the provenance, which lives in the Dataset's attributes. per_epoch=True writes one COG per epoch.

docs.title: Multiscale pyramid¶
docs.text: to_pyramid writes the input as level 0 and quality-weighted downsampled levels (downsample) as sibling groups 1, 2, ..., with the zarr-conventions multiscales layout on the root. Every level is self-contained (CRS, transform, the same variables as level 0), and open_pyramid finds the levels from the layout.

docs.title: MintPy¶
docs.text: to_mintpy writes timeseries.h5 and the quality files MintPy reads, with the platform constants of the product (wavelength, orbit height).

docs.title: Line-of-sight geometry and plate motion¶
docs.text:
DISP measures motion along the radar line of sight (LOS), positive toward the satellite. The LOS direction changes across a frame: the incidence angle grows from near to far range. Converting between east/north/up motion and LOS needs the static layers:

  • the LOS unit vector (los_east, los_north, los_up);
  • the incidence and azimuth angles derived from it;
  • the DEM;
  • the layover and shadow mask.

dxr.open_static(ds) downloads the DISP-S1-STATIC files of the frame once and puts them on the DISP grid. disp_xr geometry does the same from the command line. The docs build cannot download, so this page writes small static files in the DISP-S1-STATIC layout and passes them with files=.

docs.title: From east, north, up to LOS¶
docs.text: dxr.enu_to_los projects any motion onto the LOS. Pure vertical motion shows up scaled by the cosine of the incidence angle, so the same subsidence looks smaller in far range. Horizontal motion depends on the look direction: east-west motion is seen well, north-south hardly at all (polar orbits look east or west).

docs.title: Plate motion¶
docs.text:
GNSS velocities in a global frame (ITRF) include the rigid motion of the plate: about 2 cm/yr for North America, 5 cm/yr for the Pacific. DISP is relative to its reference pixel, so a uniform plate motion would cancel, except that the LOS changes across the frame: a uniform motion leaves a ramp in DISP. remove_plate_motion subtracts the ITRF2014 plate-motion model (Altamimi et al. 2017), projected on the LOS of each pixel, so the result is in a plate-fixed frame like plate-fixed GNSS.

This synthetic frame is only 2 km across, so the ramp is small; across a 250 km DISP-S1 frame it reaches a few mm/yr.

docs.title: Comparing DISP with GNSS¶
docs.text:
disp_xr.residuals.compare reads DISP at each GNSS station, projects the station's east, north and up motion onto the line of sight, and computes the metrics with geepers: velocities of both series from the same estimator, pairwise relative RMSE against distance, RMSE per epoch and a misfit semivariogram. disp-xr adds normalized velocity residuals, outlier and bad-epoch flags, and scores the OPERA DISP-S1 requirements.

This page uses a synthetic frame and synthetic stations that follow it, so it runs anywhere (gnss extra). One station has an extra 3 cm/yr of motion that DISP does not see, the kind of disagreement the comparison should flag.

docs.title: Compare¶
docs.text: static holds the line-of-sight vectors (from dxr.open_static on a real frame; vertical here). With no other argument, the pairwise profile is scored against the DISP-S1 displacement requirement and station pairs against the velocity requirement.

docs.title: Relative error against distance¶
docs.text: Every station pair gives the RMSE of its relative misfit over time. The binned profile carries the requirement and the fraction of pairs that pass it in each bin.

docs.title: Epochs and the misfit semivariogram¶
docs.text: The RMSE per epoch flags acquisitions where DISP disagrees with the whole network (troposphere, unwrapping); the semivariogram shows the spatial scale of the misfit.
