docs.title: Tying DISP to GNSS¶
docs.text:
Long-wavelength errors (orbits, ionosphere, troposphere left by the corrections) show up in DISP as smooth ramps that grow with time. GNSS stations measure the true motion at a few points, so the difference DISP minus GNSS at the stations samples the error. disp_xr.models.fit_tie fits a smooth field to that difference (a plane by default), and apply_tie subtracts it from DISP.

The tie holds long-wavelength error only. Stations on local deformation (a subsiding basin, a landslide) would pull the field toward their motion, so exclude= leaves them out of the fit: local signals stay in the product (remove-restore).

This page plants a known ramp in a synthetic frame and removes it.

docs.title: Fit the tie¶
docs.text: The tie is fitted on the output of compare. In epoch mode it fits one plane per epoch to the displacement residuals (weights from the GNSS sigmas); in velocity mode, one plane to the velocity residuals.

docs.title: Does it generalize? Leave one station out¶
docs.text: Each station in turn is left out, the tie is fitted on the others and the left-out station's residual is scored before and after. Smaller RMSE after means the field predicts the error where it has no station. With more flexible fields (damping= adds a spline) the scores improve partly by construction, so compare fields of similar complexity.

docs.title: Interactive browsing of a full frame¶
docs.text:
A DISP frame is about 7,000 x 9,000 pixels, more than a browser can draw as individual pixels. hvplot with datashader rasterizes the array to the size of the plot, so a whole frame stays responsive, and a slider steps through epochs. These need the interactive extra (pip install "disp_xr[interactive]"); nothing in disp-xr itself imports them.

This page is static: the slider works, and each epoch is rasterized once when the page is built. In a notebook or a panel serve app, the plot is dynamic: zooming in rasterizes again at full resolution, and only the epoch on screen is read.

docs.title: Maps through time¶
docs.text:
A symmetric color scale centered on zero, from the disp-xr diverging map. In a notebook, one call gives a dynamic plot with a time slider; only the epoch on screen is read and rasterized:

mm.hvplot.image(x="x", y="y", groupby="time", rasterize=True, cmap=..., clim=...)

This static page embeds four epochs, each rasterized once with datashader to 320 x 320 pixels, so the page stays small. (hvplot 0.12 cannot combine groupby with dynamic=False, so the frames are collected in a HoloMap.)

docs.title: Quality layers and masking¶
docs.text: Every DISP granule carries quality layers next to displacement. This example looks at them, compares the "recommended" and "strict" mask presets, and summarizes how often each pixel passes over time.

docs.title: The layers of one epoch¶
docs.text: recommended_mask is 1 where the processor recommends the pixel; water, low temporal coherence and unreliable unwrapping regions are 0.

docs.title: Mask presets¶
docs.text: mask sets displacement to NaN where a pixel fails. "strict" adds the connected-component, water and temporal-coherence criteria to the recommended mask. Criteria can also be given one by one, for example dxr.mask(ds, None, temporal_coherence=0.5). In this synthetic frame the recommended mask already excludes everything "strict" adds. A coherence threshold alone keeps more: it drops the low-coherence corner (0.3) but not the water columns, which the recommended mask removes.

docs.title: Over time¶
docs.text: quality_summary reduces over time: the share of epochs each pixel was masked, the harmonic mean of temporal coherence (which weights bad periods more than a plain mean), and whether the pixel is reliable (recommended in at least 90% of epochs).

docs.title: Quality weights¶
docs.text: quality_weights turns the DISP quality layers into one weight per pixel and epoch, between 0 and 1: a linear stretch of phase similarity and temporal coherence above a floor, and a down-weighting of dates whose inversion residuals show unwrapping cycle jumps (multiples of 2 pi). The weights feed weighted fits and, later, quality-weighted downsampling.

docs.title: Each layer and the combination¶
docs.text: Epoch 1 has injected cycle jumps at two pixels (one and two cycles), and a low-coherence corner. The combined weight is the geometric mean of the layer weights, so a pixel is only trusted when every layer is good.

docs.title: Cycle jumps down-weight, never exclude¶
docs.text: Each 2 pi cycle multiplies the residual weight by penalty (0.5), and the weight never drops below min_residual (0.05). Low coherence or similarity, below the processor's thresholds, does exclude (weight 0).

docs.title: Weighted fit¶
docs.text: Weights enter fit_trajectory as 1 / variance factors; a zero weight drops the epoch, so the excluded corner gets no velocity.

docs.title: Do residuals really cluster at 2 pi?¶
docs.text: residual_cycle_histogram counts residuals in units of 2 pi. On real DISP-S1 granules (frame F44055) the counts peak near 1, 2 and 3 cycles, which is what the cycle decomposition assumes; run it on your own frame to check.

docs.title: Quick look at a frame¶
docs.text: Open a frame of DISP granules, apply the product corrections and quality mask, chain the ministacks, re-reference, and look at a map and a time series. The granules are synthetic (disp_xr.tutorial), written with the layout of real DISP-S1 files and a known truth, so the result can be checked. Replace folder with your own granules.

docs.title: Open, correct, mask, chain¶
docs.text: open_disp reads metadata only. Corrections and the mask apply per granule, before chain chains the three ministacks into one series from the first reference date.

docs.title: Map¶
docs.text: plot_map shows one epoch (the last by default) in millimeters on a scale symmetric about zero. Masked pixels and water are blank.

docs.title: Time series¶
docs.text: plot_point takes a longitude and latitude (or row/col) and marks each reference-date change, where one ministack is joined to the next.

docs.title: Check against the truth¶
docs.text: rereference records the pixel it chose in attrs["reference"]. The synthetic truth is known, so the chaining itself can be checked: without corrections, masking or re-referencing, the chained series must equal the displacement the granules were built from.

docs.title: Corrections and reference methods¶
docs.text:
DISP displacement is relative in space and in time. In time, each granule is relative to its ministack's reference date, until chain chains them. In space, values are relative to an arbitrary point, so a map means something only after re-referencing. The order follows the product:

  1. correct: subtract correction layers, per granule (they are relative to each granule's reference date, so this comes before chaining);
  2. mask (optional);
  3. chain: chain the ministacks;
  4. rereference: choose what is zero in each epoch.

The synthetic frame has a low-coherence corner, a patch where unwrapping failed, water columns on the east edge and a few persistent scatterers, so the methods can be compared.

docs.title: Corrections¶
docs.text: correct subtracts the product's ionospheric delay and solid-earth tide ("product" in the command line picks those the product has not applied already). External corrections, such as a troposphere model, go in external= on the same grid.

docs.title: Reference methods¶
docs.text:
Method Zero in each epoch Use when point one pixel (row/col, lon/lat) a GNSS station, a stable point area median of a lon/lat box or polygon a stable region (robust) median median of the scene's good pixels the scene is mostly stable border median of a border strip deformation sits in the middle high_coherence median of a good-pixel mask you have your own mask auto a stable pixel chosen from the quality layers no prior knowledge

auto picks a pixel that is never masked, has no phase jumps, and has high harmonic-mean coherence, close to the middle of the good area. It prefers persistent scatterers. It reads every quality layer of every epoch first, which is slow on full frames (see "Large frames and batch jobs").

docs.title: A REST service for web clients¶
docs.text:
disp_xr serve STORE serves a store read-only over HTTP, for web maps and dashboards (the DISP portal, Cal/Val pages) that need more than tiles:

  • displacement series at a point,
  • the stored velocity and its sigma,
  • grid or quadtree cells of a bounding box as GeoJSON,
  • GNSS station residuals,
  • the provenance of the store.

Nothing heavy runs on request. Velocities and GNSS residuals are served when the store holds them, so they are computed once, by whoever builds the store. This page builds such a store from a synthetic frame, starts the service and queries every route, then shows a MapLibre client. Deploying the service is covered in Serving stores over HTTP.

docs.title: A store with velocity and GNSS residuals¶
docs.text: The cube, its velocity and sigma (written into the same store), and the GNSS comparison as a gnss group next to it (Comparison.to_zarr).

docs.title: Serve¶
docs.text: On the command line this is disp_xr serve demo.zarr --port 9000. Here the same application runs in a thread. The API page with every route and response schema is at /docs.

docs.title: A point: series and velocity¶
docs.text: timeseries returns the median over buffer_m at each epoch, with the quality layers the store holds. velocity reads the stored velocity at the same point.

docs.title: Cells of a bounding box¶
docs.text: cells downsamples the box on request, on a regular grid (size_m) or a quadtree (n_points), and returns GeoJSON polygons in longitude and latitude. The layer is the stored velocity if there is one, else the last displacement epoch (layer=, date= choose).

docs.title: A MapLibre client¶
docs.text:
The cells are a GeoJSON source; a click asks for the series at that point. With MapLibre GL JS:

const api = "https://your-server/datasets/demo/disp";
map.on("load", async () => {
  const b = map.getBounds();
  const bbox = [b.getWest(), b.getSouth(), b.getEast(), b.getNorth()].join(",");
  const cells = await (await fetch(`${api}/cells?bbox=${bbox}&size_m=600`)).json();
  map.addSource("cells", { type: "geojson", data: cells });
  map.addLayer({
    id: "cells", type: "fill", source: "cells",
    paint: {
      "fill-color": ["interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "velocity"],

docs.title: Velocity from a trajectory fit¶
docs.text: fit_trajectory fits every pixel with a trajectory model: offset and velocity, seasonal sine/cosine pairs, steps and postseismic terms, by least squares over each pixel's valid epochs. The synthetic frame has a known velocity, a 5 mm annual cycle and a 10 mm step, so the fit can be checked.

docs.title: Fit¶
docs.text: Trajectory lists the terms. The coefficient names encode the model, so a fit written to a store can be evaluated again with predict_trajectory.

docs.title: Velocity and its uncertainty¶
docs.text: These sigmas assume white noise; the next section compares them with colored-noise and robust estimates.

docs.title: Model and residuals at a pixel¶
docs.text: predict_trajectory evaluates the fit at any dates, lazily and in float32; the model is never stored unless you write it.

docs.title: Colored-noise and robust sigmas¶
docs.text: fit_velocity estimates the noise of every pixel (see "Choosing a velocity method" for when to use which). "whittle" keeps the OLS velocity and estimates power-law plus white noise from the periodogram of the residuals (reliable from about 200 epochs); "midas" takes the median of one-year slopes, with a deliberately conservative sigma. The synthetic noise is white, so OLS and Whittle should agree and Whittle should find kappa near 0; on real InSAR series the white-noise sigma is several times too small.

docs.title: Virtual frames and versioned stores with Icechunk¶
docs.text:
Two ways to keep a frame in Icechunk, a transactional store on top of Zarr with commits, branches and tags (cloud extra):

  • Virtual frame (build_virtual_frame): references to the chunks inside the original granules, with no data copied. Opening reads only the chunk index, so a whole frame opens in seconds, locally or on S3. Each ministack is one commit, and new granules extend the frame.
  • Native store (to_icechunk): writes your processed results (a stack, a velocity) as Zarr inside Icechunk, with appends along time and tags for releases.

Both work the same on a local folder and on S3. This page runs locally on synthetic granules. Icechunk warns that a local folder is not safe for concurrent commits from several processes, which does not apply to one script; its log level is raised to errors here.

docs.title: A virtual frame¶
docs.text: The first two ministacks go in now, and the third later, as if it had just been produced. Each call commits one snapshot per ministack.

docs.title: Time travel¶
docs.text: Every commit stays readable. Opening the frame as of the second commit gives the frame before the last ministack was added.

docs.title: A native, versioned store of results¶
docs.text: to_icechunk writes processed data with the same Zarr layout presets as to_zarr. append_dim="time" adds new epochs as a new commit, and a tag marks a release.

docs.title: Serving results as web map tiles¶
docs.text:
xpublish-tiles serves xarray datasets as OGC Tiles for any web map (MapLibre, Leaflet, QGIS): PNG tiles rendered on request from the data, a TileJSON description and a legend. A velocity map, a displacement epoch or a quality layer from disp-xr can go straight in. A Zarr or GeoZarr store from to_zarr or to_geozarr works too, with multiscale pyramids picked by zoom level.

This page fits a velocity on a synthetic frame, starts a local server and fetches a tile and the legend. In a real deployment the server runs behind your web map (see the end).

docs.title: Serve¶
docs.text: xpublish.Rest serves named datasets; TilesPlugin adds the tile endpoints under /datasets/<name>/tiles/.

docs.title: A tile and its legend¶
docs.text: The tile covering the frame center at zoom 13, rendered with a fixed color range so tiles match across the map.

docs.title: On a web map¶
docs.text:
Point a raster source at the tile URL template. With MapLibre GL JS:

map.addSource("velocity", {
  "type": "raster",
  tiles: ["https://your-server/datasets/velocity/tiles/WebMercatorQuad/{z}/{y}/{x}"
          + "?variables=velocity&style=raster/RdBu&colorscalerange=-30,30"
          + "&width=256&height=256"],
  tileSize: 256,
});
map.addLayer({ id: "velocity", type: "raster", source: "velocity" });

{base}/tilejson.json with the same parameters describes the layer (bounds, zooms) for clients that read TileJSON. To serve a whole frame, open its store lazily (xr.open_zarr, or a pyramid from to_geozarr): tiles read only the chunks they cover.

docs.title: Comparing two processing versions of a frame¶
docs.text:
Frame F08622 (New York City and Long Island), 2016-07 to 2024-12: the same 239 acquisitions processed as product version 1.0 and as 1.1. A new processing version changes the algorithm, not the data, so the two should agree within noise wherever the ground is coherent. This notebook puts them on a common footing (same epochs, same reference) and looks at where they differ: the maps at the last date, the velocities, a few pixel series and the scatter around the reference.

This notebook ran on real granules; its outputs are saved, and the documentation build does not run it again.

docs.title: Ministacks¶
docs.text: Both versions cover the same 239 acquisitions in 16 ministacks. Their reference dates agree except the second: v1.0 starts it on 2017-03-13 and v1.1 on 2016-09-26, so the two chain the first year differently. The table lists the first ministack reference dates of each.

docs.title: A common footing¶
docs.text: A 30 x 30 km window over Brooklyn, Queens and lower Manhattan, chained per version, kept to the epochs both have, and referenced to the same 1 km box in Brooklyn.

docs.title: Velocities¶
docs.text: MIDAS velocity of each version on the pixels valid in at least half the common epochs in both.

docs.title: Series at four points¶
docs.text: The median of a 30 m radius around each point (about one pixel and its neighbors): LaGuardia Airport, lower Manhattan, Woodside and Ridgewood.

docs.title: Scatter around the reference¶
docs.text: With the reference box assumed stable, the spread of the pixels within 1 km of it, epoch by epoch, is a direct look at each version's noise at short distance.

docs.title: What changed¶
docs.text:
• Where the ground is coherent, the two versions agree within their noise.
    • At the last date, on the 66% of pixels valid in both: a median difference of -0.2 mm, spread 0.4 mm (1.4826 MAD).
    • In velocity: a median difference of -0.01 mm/yr, spread 0.08 mm/yr. Only 0.2% of the pixels differ by more than 2 mm/yr, isolated pixels scattered across the window.
  • LaGuardia Airport is the one point of the four where the series part: from about 2019, v1.1 sits a few millimetres above v1.0.
  • v1.1 is quieter near the reference. The pixel spread within 1 km of it has a median of 5.1 mm, against 5.6 mm for v1.0, and is lower at almost every epoch.
